subject: sci
title: Human Body and Health: Body Systems, Homeostasis, Nutrition, and Disease
objectives: You will identify the major human body systems, name their main organs and jobs, and explain how two or more systems work together.
You will explain homeostasis and trace a feedback loop (stimulus, receptor, control center, effector, response), telling negative feedback from positive feedback.
You will read a Nutrition Facts label and calculate Calories from carbohydrate, protein, and fat (4, 4, and 9 Calories per gram).
You will classify diseases as infectious or noninfectious, compare types of pathogens, and explain how the immune system and vaccines provide protection.
You will interpret health data in tables and graphs, including rates per 100,000 people, and choose conclusions the data support.

slides.title: Human Body and Health: Systems, Balance, Food, and Disease
slides.board:
Today you will:

  • Name the major body systems and show how they work together
  • Trace a feedback loop and tell negative feedback from positive feedback
  • Use 4-4-9 and a Nutrition Facts label to calculate Calories
  • Explain how pathogens cause disease and how immunity and vaccines protect you
  • Read health data and choose conclusions the data support

Plan: Warm-up → 7 big ideas → practice together → your turn → GED-style questions

notes.say: This week we move from the single cell to the whole human body. Human body and health is one of the biggest parts of life science on the GED Science test, and the questions are rarely about memorizing organ names. They hand you a short description, a nutrition label, or a health data table, and they ask you to reason with it. Today you will learn the core ideas and a routine for each question type, so you can walk into any body or health question with a plan.
ask: Think about the last time you exercised hard. What changed in your body? (expected answer: faster heartbeat, faster breathing, sweating, tired muscles; keep the list, because we will match each change to a body system)
notes.watch: Keep all health content general. If the student raises a personal health concern, acknowledge it and suggest talking with a doctor; this lesson teaches how the body works and how to read health data, not personal medical or diet advice.

slides.title: Warm-Up: Cells Review (Week 3)
slides.board:
1. Which organelle carries out cellular respiration?
  2. What are the two reactants of photosynthesis (besides light energy)?
  3. Which structure is found in plant cells but not in animal cells: mitochondrion, chloroplast, nucleus, or cell membrane?
  4. Your leg muscles need oxygen and glucose to keep working. Which cell process uses both, and what useful product does it make?
steps: 1. The mitochondrion (plural: mitochondria).
2. Carbon dioxide and water: 6CO2 + 6H2O + light → C6H12O6 + 6O2.
3. The chloroplast. Both plant and animal cells have mitochondria, a nucleus, and a cell membrane.
4. Cellular respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy stored as ATP.

notes.say: These four questions review last week's lesson on cells and energy. Give the student about two minutes, then have them tell you each answer before you reveal it. Number 4 is the bridge into today: every body system we study exists, in part, to deliver oxygen and glucose to cells and carry away the carbon dioxide they make.
ask: Where does the glucose in your muscle cells originally come from? (expected answer: from food, broken down by the digestive system; ultimately from photosynthesis in plants)
Which waste gas does cellular respiration make, and how does your body get rid of it? (expected answer: carbon dioxide; the blood carries it to the lungs and you breathe it out)
notes.answer: 1. Mitochondrion. 2. Carbon dioxide and water. 3. Chloroplast. 4. Cellular respiration; it makes ATP (plus carbon dioxide and water).
notes.watch: Students often swap the two processes. Quick check: photosynthesis makes glucose and releases oxygen; respiration uses glucose and oxygen to release energy.

slides.title: Big Idea 1: From Cells to Body Systems
slides.board:
Cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism

SystemKey partsMain job
CirculatoryHeart, blood vessels, bloodTransports O2, nutrients, hormones, wastes
RespiratoryTrachea, lungsTakes in O2; removes CO2
DigestiveStomach, intestines, liverBreaks down food; absorbs nutrients
ExcretoryKidneys, bladderFilters blood; balances water
NervousBrain, spinal cord, nervesSenses and signals; fast control
EndocrineGlands (pancreas, thyroid)Hormones; slower control
ImmuneWhite blood cells, lymph nodesFights pathogens
Muscular / skeletalMuscles, bonesMovement, support
IntegumentarySkinBarrier; cooling

notes.say: Your body is organized in levels. Muscle cells form muscle tissue; muscle tissue plus other tissues form an organ such as the heart; the heart and blood vessels form the circulatory system. You do not need every detail on this table, but you do need to match each system to its job, because GED questions ask which system is most directly responsible for something. Notice the two control systems: the nervous system sends fast electrical signals along nerves, and the endocrine system sends slower chemical messages, called hormones, through the blood.
ask: Which level comes between cells and organs? (expected answer: tissues)
Which two systems control and coordinate the others? (expected answer: nervous and endocrine)
notes.watch: Students mix up the trachea (air, respiratory) and the esophagus (food, digestive) because both are in the throat. Ask: "Does it carry air or food?"

slides.title: Worked Example: Follow the Oxygen
slides.board: You climb a flight of stairs. Trace one breath of oxygen from the air to a working leg muscle, and name each system it passes through.
steps: Air flows in through the nose and trachea to the lungs. In tiny air sacs (alveoli), oxygen crosses into the blood. Respiratory system.
Red blood cells pick up the oxygen. The heart pumps this oxygen-rich blood through arteries to the leg. Circulatory system.
Muscle cells take in the oxygen and use it in cellular respiration to release energy from glucose as ATP. Muscular system.
The carbon dioxide the muscle makes rides the blood back to the lungs and is breathed out. Three systems, one job: keep the muscle working.

notes.say: Watch how one molecule of oxygen depends on several systems. The respiratory system loads oxygen into the blood, but it cannot deliver it; the circulatory system delivers it, but it cannot pick it up from the air. This is what the GED means by systems working together. When a question asks which system is most directly responsible, find the exact step the question is about.
ask: The lungs and the heart both handle oxygen. Which one moves it to the leg? (expected answer: the heart, part of the circulatory system)
Where does the glucose the muscle burns come from? (expected answer: food broken down by the digestive system and carried by the blood)

slides.title: We Do: Which Systems Are Working?
slides.board:
Name the systems at work in each case.

  1. You eat a sandwich, and an hour later its nutrients reach your arm muscles.
  2. You touch a hot pan and pull your hand away before you even think about it.
  3. After a long, hot run, your kidneys make less urine.
steps: 1. Digestive (stomach and small intestine break the food down and absorb the nutrients) and circulatory (blood carries the nutrients to the arm).
2. Nervous (receptors in the skin, nerves, and the spinal cord send the signal) and muscular/skeletal (arm muscles pull the bones to move the hand).
3. Excretory (kidneys save water), directed by the nervous and endocrine systems: the brain detects the water loss and a hormone signals the kidneys. This is homeostasis, our next big idea.

notes.say: Let's work through these together. For each one, tell me what happens first, then what happens next, and name the system for each step. The third one is a preview: the body noticed it was low on water and corrected it. Hold on to that idea, because it is the heart of the next slide.
ask: In number 1, where are most nutrients absorbed? (expected answer: the small intestine)
In number 2, why does the hand move before you think? (expected answer: it is a reflex; the spinal cord sends the signal straight back to the muscles)
notes.answer: 1. Digestive + circulatory. 2. Nervous + muscular/skeletal. 3. Excretory, controlled by nervous + endocrine (the hormone is ADH, antidiuretic hormone; the name is not required on the GED).
notes.watch: For number 3, students may say "digestive" because water is something you drink. The kidneys filter blood and make urine, so this is the excretory system.

slides.title: Big Idea 2: Homeostasis and the Feedback Loop
slides.board:
Homeostasis: keeping internal conditions stable while the outside world changes.

Examples: body temperature near 37 °C (98.6 °F); blood glucose in a normal range; enough water.

Stimulus (a change) → Receptor (detects it) → Control center (compares to the set point; often the brain) → Effector (muscle, gland, or organ that acts) → Response

notes.say: Homeostasis is the body's thermostat. Each condition has a set point, a normal value, and when something pushes the condition away from it, the body detects the change and responds. Every feedback loop has the same five parts, and GED questions often ask you to name one of them. The receptor detects, the control center decides, and the effector acts. A simple test: the effector is the part that does the work, such as a muscle that shivers, a gland that releases sweat or a hormone, or an organ such as the kidneys saving water.
ask: On a hot day, what is the effector that cools you? (expected answer: sweat glands)
What is the control center for body temperature? (expected answer: the brain, specifically the hypothalamus)
notes.watch: Students call the brain the receptor whenever it appears. The brain usually compares and decides, so it is the control center; receptors are sensors, often in the skin or blood vessels.

slides.title: Worked Example: Label the Blood-Sugar Loop
slides.board:
Two hours after lunch, Dana's blood glucose is higher than normal. Cells in her pancreas detect the rise and release insulin into the blood. Insulin signals muscle, liver, and fat cells to take in glucose. Her blood glucose falls back into the normal range, and the pancreas releases less insulin.

Label each part of the loop.
steps: Stimulus: blood glucose rises above normal after a meal.
Receptor and control center: cells in the pancreas. Here one organ both detects the rise and sets how much insulin to release.
Messenger: insulin, a hormone (endocrine system), carried in the blood (circulatory system).
Effectors: muscle, liver, and fat cells take in glucose. Response: blood glucose falls back toward normal.
Type: negative feedback. The response reverses the change, and once glucose is normal, insulin release slows.

notes.say: This loop shows up on the GED again and again. Notice that the control center does not have to be the brain; in this loop the pancreas does the detecting and the deciding. Also notice the opposite hormone: when blood glucose drops too low, the pancreas releases glucagon, which tells the liver to release stored glucose. Insulin lowers, glucagon raises.
ask: What hormone would the pancreas release if Dana skipped breakfast and her glucose dropped? (expected answer: glucagon)
Why does insulin release slow down at the end? (expected answer: the stimulus, high glucose, is gone)

slides.title: Big Idea 3: Negative vs. Positive Feedback
slides.board:
Negative feedbackPositive feedback
What it doesReverses the change, back toward the set pointIncreases the change until an event ends it
How commonMost homeostasisA few special processes
ExamplesSweating, shivering, insulin, glucagon, kidneys saving water, faster breathing when CO2 risesChildbirth contractions (oxytocin), blood clotting at a cut

Memory aid: Negative = "No, go back." Positive = "More, more, more."

notes.say: The words negative and positive do not mean bad and good here. They describe direction. Negative feedback pushes in the opposite direction of the change, so it brings the body back to normal; that is how nearly all homeostasis works. Positive feedback pushes in the same direction, so the change keeps growing until some event ends it, such as a baby being born or a cut being sealed. To decide, compare the direction of the change with the direction of the response.
ask: Is negative feedback harmful? (expected answer: no; it keeps conditions normal)
What ends the positive feedback loop of clotting? (expected answer: the cut is sealed)
notes.watch: The biggest trap: students hear "negative" and think "bad." Make them say the rule: negative means the response goes the opposite way from the change.

slides.title: Worked Example: Negative or Positive?
slides.board:
During a run, carbon dioxide (CO2) builds up in the blood. Sensors in the brainstem and in large arteries detect the rise. The brain signals the diaphragm and rib muscles to work faster. Breathing speeds up, extra CO2 is breathed out, and blood CO2 falls back toward normal.

Negative or positive feedback?
steps: The change: blood CO2 goes up.
The response: faster breathing removes CO2, so blood CO2 goes down.
Opposite directions, so the response reverses the change: negative feedback.
Contrast: in positive feedback the response would push CO<sub>2</sub> even higher, and nothing would stop it until some outside event did.

notes.say: Here is the two-arrow method. Draw one arrow for the change and one for the response. If the arrows point opposite ways, it is negative feedback; if they point the same way, it is positive. Notice that the description never uses the word feedback, which is typical of GED passages. You have to figure it out from the directions.
ask: In this loop, what are the effectors? (expected answer: the diaphragm and rib muscles)
Which two systems are working together here? (expected answer: nervous and respiratory, with the circulatory system carrying the CO2)

slides.title: We Do: Label the Cold-Day Loop
slides.board:
A person walks outside on a freezing day. Nerve endings in the skin detect the cold. The hypothalamus in the brain sends signals to skeletal muscles, which begin to shiver, and to blood vessels in the skin, which narrow. Shivering produces heat, less heat escapes through the skin, and body temperature stays near normal.

Name the stimulus, receptor, control center, effectors, response, and type.
steps: Stimulus: cold air starts to lower body temperature. Receptor: nerve endings in the skin.
Control center: the hypothalamus (brain). Effectors: skeletal muscles and skin blood vessels.
Response: shivering makes heat and narrowed vessels keep heat in. Type: negative feedback, because warming reverses the cooling.

notes.say: Now you lead. Read the passage with me and stop me each time we reach a part of the loop. Notice there are two effectors here: the muscles that shiver and the blood vessels that narrow. Both push body temperature back up, which is the opposite of the change, so we know the type.
ask: Which word in the passage tells you the receptor? (expected answer: detect)
On a hot day, what do the skin blood vessels do instead? (expected answer: widen, so more heat escapes through the skin)
notes.answer: Stimulus: cold lowering body temperature. Receptor: skin nerve endings. Control center: hypothalamus. Effectors: skeletal muscles and skin blood vessels. Response: heat produced and kept in; temperature stays near 37 °C. Type: negative feedback.
notes.watch: Some students name "cold air" as the receptor. The receptor is the body part that detects the change, not the change itself.

slides.title: Your Turn: Systems and Feedback
slides.board:
1. The pancreas releases insulin. Which system carries the insulin to cells all over the body?
  2. At a cut, platelets stick to the wound and release chemicals that attract more platelets, until a clot seals the cut. Negative or positive feedback?
  3. A person is dehydrated. The brain detects low water, a hormone signals the kidneys, and the kidneys return more water to the blood, so less urine is made. Name the effector and the type of feedback.
steps: 1. The circulatory system (the blood). Insulin itself is an endocrine hormone.
2. Positive feedback: more platelets attract still more platelets until the clot ends the process.
3. Effector: the kidneys. Type: negative feedback, because saving water reverses the water loss.

notes.say: Work these alone; you have three minutes. Tell me your answer and your reason for each one, and I will reveal only after you commit. Use the two-arrow method on numbers 2 and 3.
notes.answer: 1. Circulatory system. 2. Positive feedback. 3. Effector: kidneys; negative feedback.
notes.watch: On number 1, students may answer "endocrine" because insulin is a hormone. The question asks what carries it: the blood. On number 3, the brain is the control center, not the effector.

slides.title: Big Idea 4: Nutrition and the 4-4-9 Rule
slides.board:
Carbohydrate 4  |  Protein 4  |  Fat 9  Calories per gram

  • Vitamins, minerals, and water supply no Calories, but you still need them.
  • Every number on a Nutrition Facts label is for one serving. Multiply by the servings actually eaten.
  • % Daily Value (2,000-Calorie basis): 5% or less = low; 20% or more = high.
  • Energy balance: take in more Calories than you use and the extra is stored, mostly as fat; use more and stored energy is burned.

notes.say: Food gives the body two things: energy and building materials. Energy in food is measured in Calories; a food Calorie with a capital C is a kilocalorie. Only three nutrients supply energy, and you must know their numbers cold: 4, 4, and 9. Fat packs more than twice the energy per gram of carbohydrate or protein. The single most common GED trap on labels is servings, so the first thing you read on any label is servings per container.
ask: How many Calories are in 10 grams of fat? (expected answer: 90)
A serving has 3% of the Daily Value for sodium. Low or high? (expected answer: low, because it is 5% or less)
notes.watch: Students use 4 for fat because two of the three numbers are 4. Have them write 4-4-9 at the top of their scratch paper before any label question.

slides.title: Worked Example: Calories on a Label
slides.board:
Yogurt label: Serving size 1 cup (227 g)  |  Servings per container 2  |  Calories 150  |  Total fat 2 g  |  Total carbohydrate 20 g  |  Protein 13 g

a) Find the Calories from each nutrient in one serving and check the total.
b) How many Calories are in the whole container?
steps: Fat: 2 g × 9 = 18 Calories.
Carbohydrate: 20 g × 4 = 80 Calories. Protein: 13 g × 4 = 52 Calories.
Check: 18 + 80 + 52 = 150 Calories, which matches the label.
Whole container: 2 servings × 150 = 300 Calories (and 2 × 13 = 26 g of protein).

notes.say: This is the label routine. Step one, circle servings per container. Step two, multiply each nutrient by its 4-4-9 number. Step three, add and compare with the label's Calorie line; real labels round, so a small difference is normal. Step four, multiply by the number of servings actually eaten.
ask: Why multiply by 2 in the last step? (expected answer: the container holds 2 servings and every label number is for one serving)

slides.title: Worked Example: Percent of Calories and %DV
slides.board:
Same yogurt: 150 Calories per serving, 13 g protein. The label also lists Calcium 30% DV and Sodium 5% DV per serving.

a) What percent of the Calories in one serving come from protein?
b) Someone eats the whole container. Rate the calcium and sodium as low, moderate, or high.
steps: Protein Calories: 13 × 4 = 52.
Percent from protein: 52 ÷ 150 = 0.3466… ≈ 35%.
Whole container = 2 servings. Calcium: 2 × 30% = 60% DV, high (20% or more).
Sodium: 2 × 5% = 10% DV, moderate (between 5% and 20%).

notes.say: Two different percents live on nutrition questions, and students confuse them. Percent of Calories compares one nutrient's Calories with the total Calories in the food. Percent Daily Value compares the nutrient with a whole day's recommended amount. Both get multiplied when the person eats more than one serving.
ask: Why can't you find the percent from protein by doing 13 divided by 150? (expected answer: 13 is grams; you must convert to Calories first, 13 times 4)
notes.watch: Watch for 13 ÷ 150 ≈ 9%. That divides grams by Calories. Convert grams to Calories first.

slides.title: We Do: The Cracker Label
slides.board:
Crackers: Serving size 3 crackers (30 g)  |  Servings per container 8  |  Calories 140  |  Total fat 5 g  |  Total carbohydrate 21 g  |  Protein 2 g  |  Sodium 230 mg (10% DV)

  1. Calories from fat in one serving?
  2. Show that the 140-Calorie total is about right.
  3. Someone eats 9 crackers. How many servings and Calories?
  4. Is one serving low, moderate, or high in sodium?
steps: 1. 5 g × 9 = 45 Calories.
2. 45 + (21 × 4 = 84) + (2 × 4 = 8) = 137 Calories. Labels round, so 137 ≈ 140.
3. 9 ÷ 3 = 3 servings; 3 × 140 = 420 Calories.
4. Moderate: 10% is between 5% (low) and 20% (high).

notes.say: Let's do this one together. You tell me what to multiply, and I will write. Number 3 is the classic GED move: the serving is measured in crackers, so first turn crackers into servings, then multiply.
ask: In number 3, what do you do first? (expected answer: divide 9 crackers by 3 crackers per serving)
What would 9 × 140 mean, and why is it wrong? (expected answer: it treats each cracker as a serving; one serving is 3 crackers)
notes.watch: If the student gets 1,260 on number 3, they multiplied 9 × 140. Point to the serving size: 3 crackers.

slides.title: Your Turn: Label Math
slides.board:
1. A food has 12 g of fat per serving. How many Calories come from fat?
  2. A snack has 7 g fat, 15 g carbohydrate, and 4 g protein per serving. Total Calories?
  3. A container holds 2.5 servings of 120 Calories each. Calories in the whole container?
  4. One serving has 25% DV of saturated fat. Low, moderate, or high?
steps: 1. 12 × 9 = 108 Calories.
2. 63 + 60 + 16 = 139 Calories (7 × 9, 15 × 4, 4 × 4).
3. 2.5 × 120 = 300 Calories.
4. High (20% or more).

notes.say: Four minutes, on your own. Write 4-4-9 at the top of your paper first. Read me each answer when you finish, and tell me what you multiplied.
notes.watch: On number 2, check that the student used 9 only for fat. A total of 104 means 4 was used for everything.

slides.title: Big Idea 5: Disease and Pathogens
slides.board:
Infectious disease: caused by a pathogen; can spread. Noninfectious: cannot be caught (type 2 diabetes, most heart disease); linked to genes, lifestyle, environment, age.

PathogenWhat it isExamplesAntibiotics?
BacteriaLiving single cells, no nucleusStrep throat, tuberculosisYes
VirusNot a cell; copies itself only inside host cellsCold, flu, measlesNo
FungusYeasts, moldsAthlete's foot, ringwormNo (antifungals)
ParasiteProtists, wormsMalaria, tapewormNo (other medicines)

Spread: droplets, touch, food/water, vectors (mosquitoes, ticks).

notes.say: The first question to ask about any disease is whether it can spread from person to person. If it can, a pathogen causes it. The four kinds of pathogens differ in ways that matter for treatment. Bacteria are living cells, so antibiotics can attack their cell parts. Viruses are not cells at all; they hijack your own cells to make copies, so antibiotics have nothing to attack. Taking antibiotics when they are not needed also helps resistant bacteria survive and spread, which is called antibiotic resistance.
ask: Will antibiotics cure the flu? Why or why not? (expected answer: no; flu is caused by a virus, and antibiotics work only on bacteria)
What is a vector? (expected answer: an animal, such as a mosquito or tick, that carries a pathogen from one host to another)
notes.watch: Ringworm is a fungus, not a worm. Use it as a reminder to read what the pathogen is, not what its name sounds like.

slides.title: Worked Example: Name the Pathogen
slides.board:
A patient has a sore throat and fever. A lab grows tiny round cells from a throat swab. The cells have a cell membrane and a cell wall but no nucleus.

What type of pathogen is this, and could an antibiotic help?
steps: Are they cells? Yes, so it is not a virus (viruses are not cells).
No nucleus means a prokaryote (Week 3). Prokaryotic pathogens are bacteria.
Fungi and parasites such as protists have a nucleus, so they are ruled out.
Bacteria are living cells, so an antibiotic can help. A sore throat caused by these bacteria is strep throat.

notes.say: This is a classic elimination question, and it pulls in last week's cell lesson. Work down the list: cell or not cell, nucleus or no nucleus. Each answer rules out a pathogen type. Then treatment follows from the type.
ask: What if the lab found no cells, only particles that multiply inside the patient's own cells? (expected answer: a virus; antibiotics would not help)

slides.title: Big Idea 6: Immunity and Vaccines
slides.board:
1. Barriers: skin, mucus, tears, stomach acid.
  2. General defenses: inflammation, fever, white blood cells that engulf invaders.
  3. Targeted defenses: white blood cells make antibodies that fit one specific pathogen; memory cells remain, so the next response is faster and stronger. That is immunity.

Vaccine: a harmless form or piece of a pathogen; the body builds memory cells without having the disease.

Community immunity: when most people are immune, the pathogen struggles to spread.

notes.say: Think of immunity as three layers. Most germs never get past the barriers. Those that do meet general defenses, which attack anything foreign. The third layer is targeted: the immune system learns the specific pathogen, makes antibodies that fit it, and keeps memory cells. A vaccine gives the immune system that practice run without the illness. And when enough people are immune, the pathogen runs out of people to infect, which protects people who cannot be vaccinated.
ask: What is the difference between an antibody and an antibiotic? (expected answer: antibodies are proteins your body makes against a specific pathogen; antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria)
Why can a person who had chickenpox usually fight it off quickly later? (expected answer: memory cells from the first infection respond fast)
notes.watch: Memory trick: antibody is made by your body. Antibiotic is a medicine against bacteria.

slides.title: Worked Example: First vs. Second Exposure
slides.board:
Antibody level in the blood (arbitrary units) after a person's first and second exposure to the same pathogen:

Days after exposure05101520
First exposure02253018
Second exposure5150240210170

Compare the two responses and explain the difference.
steps: Speed: on day 5, the level is 2 after the first exposure but 150 after the second. The second response starts much faster.
Size: the first peak is 30 (day 15); the second peak is 240 (day 10). 240 ÷ 30 = 8 times as high.
Explanation: the first exposure left memory cells. They recognize the pathogen and trigger antibody production quickly.
Connection: a vaccine acts as a safe "first exposure," so a real infection gets the fast second response.

notes.say: GED questions on immunity often come with exactly this kind of table or graph. Compare two things: how fast the response starts and how high it goes. Then explain it with memory cells. Notice the second exposure starts at 5, not 0, because some antibodies were still around from the first time.
ask: On which day did the second response peak? (expected answer: day 10)

slides.title: Big Idea 7: Reading Health Data
slides.board:
• Rate per 100,000 = cases ÷ population × 100,000. Rates let you compare places of different sizes.
  • Mean = sum ÷ count. Change = new − old. Percent change = change ÷ old × 100.
  • Pattern is not proof: two things that change together (correlation) may both be caused by something else.
  • Stay inside the data: watch for all, always, proves, permanently, or groups that were never studied.

notes.say: Almost every health question on the GED comes with data, and the math is always one of a few moves: read a value, find a change, find a mean, find a rate, or find a percent. The harder part is the conclusion. The best-supported answer describes what the data show for the people studied. Wrong answers claim more: they say proves, they talk about everyone, or they turn a pattern into a cause.
ask: Town A has 20 cases and Town B has 40 cases. Can you say Town B has the bigger problem? (expected answer: not yet; you need the populations to compare rates)
notes.watch: Students pick the most dramatic answer. Train the question "Did they measure that?" for every choice.

slides.title: Worked Example: Compare Two Towns
slides.board:
Last year, Town A (population 60,000) reported 30 cases of a foodborne illness. Town B (population 150,000) reported 45 cases.

Which town had the higher rate of illness?
steps: Town A: 30 ÷ 60,000 × 100,000 = 50 cases per 100,000.
Town B: 45 ÷ 150,000 × 100,000 = 30 cases per 100,000.
Town B had more cases (45 > 30), but Town A had the higher rate (50 > 30).
Why it matters: Town B is 2.5 times as large, so more cases there do not mean a person was more likely to get sick.

notes.say: This is why health data uses rates. Raw counts depend on how many people live somewhere. Divide by the population to get a per-person chance, then multiply by 100,000 so the number is easy to read. On the calculator, enter it in that order: cases, divide, population, times 100,000.
ask: How many cases would Town B need to match Town A's rate? (expected answer: 75, because 50 per 100,000 times 1.5 = 75)

slides.title: We Do: The Heart-Rate Table
slides.board:
One person's heart rate during and after a 6-minute treadmill walk:

TimeHeart rate (bpm)
Before walking (rest)70
End of minute 298
End of minute 4112
End of minute 6116
2 minutes after stopping84
  1. Increase from rest to the end of minute 6?
  2. Percent increase?
  3. Describe the pattern and explain it.
  4. What is one limit of this data?
steps: 1. 116 − 70 = 46 bpm.
2. 46 ÷ 70 = 0.657… ≈ 66%.
3. It rose fast (+28), then slower (+14, +4), then fell after stopping. Working muscles need more oxygen, so the heart pumps faster; afterward, negative feedback brings it back toward rest.
4. One person on one day: we cannot apply these exact numbers to everyone.

notes.say: Let's read this table together using the data routine: title, units, then the exact rows we need. For the percent, divide the change by the starting value, not by the ending value. Then tie the pattern to the body systems from Big Idea 1.
ask: For the percent increase, what do we divide by? (expected answer: the starting value, 70)
Which systems explain the rise? (expected answer: circulatory and respiratory supplying oxygen to the muscular system, controlled by the nervous system)
notes.answer: 1. 46 bpm. 2. About 66%. 3. Rapid rise, then leveling off, then recovery; muscles need more oxygen, and negative feedback returns the rate toward resting. 4. A sample of one person.
notes.watch: A student who gets about 40% divided 46 by 116, the ending value. Percent change always divides by the starting value.

slides.title: Your Turn: Pathogens and Data
slides.board:
1. Lyme disease bacteria are carried from deer and mice to people by ticks. What is the tick's role called?
  2. A friend has the flu and asks for leftover antibiotics. Give the science reason they will not help.
  3. A county of 40,000 people reported 18 cases of a disease. What is the rate per 100,000?
  4. In one city, months with more ice cream sales also have more drownings. Does ice cream cause drowning?
steps: 1. A vector.
2. Flu is caused by a virus. Antibiotics attack bacterial cell parts; viruses are not cells.
3. 18 ÷ 40,000 × 100,000 = 45 per 100,000.
4. No. Hot weather increases both ice cream sales and swimming. A pattern is not proof of cause.

notes.say: Last independent set. Four minutes. For number 3, use the calculator in the order cases, divide, population, times 100,000. For number 4, ask yourself what else could make both numbers go up.
notes.answer: 1. Vector. 2. Flu is viral; antibiotics only work on bacteria. 3. 45 per 100,000. 4. No; a third factor (hot weather) drives both.
notes.watch: On number 3, an answer of 0.00045 means the student stopped before multiplying by 100,000.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Calcium Control
slides.board:
When blood calcium drops below normal, the parathyroid glands release parathyroid hormone (PTH). PTH causes bones to release calcium into the blood and the kidneys to keep more calcium. When blood calcium returns to normal, PTH release slows.

Which statement best describes this process?

A. It is positive feedback, because PTH release increases when calcium falls.
B. It is negative feedback, because the response raises calcium back toward normal.
C. It is positive feedback, because calcium is added to the blood, which increases the level.
D. It is not a feedback loop, because bones and kidneys are not part of the endocrine system.
steps: A is out. A hormone level rising is not what makes feedback positive. Compare the change (calcium down) with the response (calcium up): they are opposite.
C is out. The level does increase, but only back to normal after it fell. Positive feedback would push calcium further in the direction it was already going, which here is down.
D is out. Effectors do not have to be glands. Bones and kidneys are the effectors that a hormone signals, which is how many feedback loops work.
B is correct. Calcium fell, and the response brought it back up toward the set point, then shut off. That is negative feedback.

notes.say: You have probably never studied parathyroid hormone, and that is the point. The GED gives you an unfamiliar loop and tests whether you can apply the rule. Use the two arrows: change down, response up. Then go through each choice and say out loud why it fails before you pick the answer.
ask: What made choices A and C tempting? (expected answer: they use the word increase, which sounds like positive)
notes.answer: B. The response reverses the drop in calcium and stops once calcium is normal: negative feedback.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Best-Supported Conclusion
slides.board:
Researchers recorded how many hours 150 healthy adults slept each night for 2 weeks. Then each adult was exposed to a common cold virus, and researchers recorded who developed a cold. (Hypothetical data.)

Average sleepLess than 6 h6 to 7 hMore than 7 h
Developed a cold32%22%15%

Which conclusion is best supported?

A. Sleeping more than 7 hours a night prevents colds.
B. Having a cold causes people to sleep fewer hours.
C. In this study, adults who slept more were less likely to develop a cold.
D. Sleep had no clear relationship to whether people developed a cold.
steps: A is out. 15% of the adults who slept more than 7 hours still caught a cold. "Prevents" goes beyond the data.
B is out. Sleep was measured before anyone was exposed, so the colds could not have caused the sleep pattern.
D is out. The percent drops steadily, 32% → 22% → 15%, as sleep increases. That is a clear pattern.
C is correct. It describes the pattern for the people studied without claiming more.

notes.say: This is the most common data question on GED Science. The right answer is usually the careful one: it names who was studied and describes the pattern. Check each wrong answer for the reason it fails: too strong, reversed cause and effect, or contradicting the numbers.
ask: What other factor might explain the pattern? (expected answer: stress, overall health, or age could affect both sleep and catching colds)
notes.answer: C. It describes the trend in the data for the adults studied. A overstates, B reverses the timing, and D contradicts the numbers.

slides.title: Test Strategy: Set Up Before You Solve
slides.board:
Before you read the answer choices:

Label? Write 4-4-9 and circle servings per container and serving size.

Table or graph? Read the title, the units, and find the exact row and column.

Feedback? Draw two arrows: change, then response.

Conclusion? Ask of each choice: Did they measure that?

notes.say: This is the habit I want you to take into the test. Spend fifteen to twenty seconds setting up before you look at the choices. Many wrong answers on health questions are the right method applied to the wrong number, such as one serving instead of the whole package, or the right idea stretched too far, such as a pattern turned into proof. Your setup catches both. You have an on-screen calculator on the Science test, so use it for every multiplication and every rate.
ask: What is the first thing you look at on a nutrition label? (expected answer: servings per container and serving size)

slides.title: Recap and What Comes Next
slides.board:
1. Cells → tissues → organs → systems. Systems work together; the nervous and endocrine systems coordinate them.
  2. Feedback loop: stimulus → receptor → control center → effector → response. Negative reverses; positive increases.
  3. 4-4-9, and multiply by servings eaten. %DV: 5% low, 20% high.
  4. Antibiotics work on bacteria, not viruses. Antibodies and memory cells give immunity; vaccines build it safely.

Next: Student Lesson → Practice (Set A) → Exit Check

Then do Practice Set A; if you score under 80 percent, take Set B. Finish with the Exit Check, where you need 6 of 8.

How many Calories are in 5 g of fat plus 10 g of protein? (expected answer: 45 + 40 = 85)

screens.title: What you will learn
screens.html:
Your body is a team of systems that work together every second to keep you alive and steady. On the GED Science test, human body and health questions give you a short description, a nutrition label, or a health data table and ask you to reason with it. In this lesson you will learn to:

  • Name the major body systems, their organs, and their jobs, and explain how they work together.
  • Explain homeostasis and trace a feedback loop, telling negative feedback from positive feedback.
  • Use the 4-4-9 rule and a Nutrition Facts label to calculate Calories.
  • Tell infectious from noninfectious disease, compare pathogens, and explain how immunity and vaccines protect you.
  • Read health data and choose conclusions the data support.

Each screen teaches one idea and ends with a quick check. Use the hint if you get stuck.

screens.title: Levels of organization
screens.html:
Your body is built in levels, from smallest to largest:

Cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism

  • A tissue is a group of similar cells doing one job, such as muscle tissue.
  • An organ is made of several tissues working together, such as the stomach or the heart.
  • An organ system is a group of organs that share one major job, such as the digestive system.

Example: heart muscle cells form heart muscle tissue; that tissue, plus nerve and connective tissue, forms the heart; the heart, blood vessels, and blood form the circulatory system.

check.prompt: The stomach contains muscle tissue that churns food, gland tissue that releases digestive juices, and nerve tissue that controls it. At which level of organization is the stomach?
options: An organ
A tissue
An organ system
A cell
why: A tissue is one kind of similar cells doing one job. The stomach contains several different tissues, which makes it the next level up.
The organ system is the whole digestive system: mouth, esophagus, stomach, intestines, and more. The stomach is one organ in it.
A cell is the smallest level. The stomach is made of millions of cells grouped into tissues.
check.hint: Several different tissues working together form which level?
check.explain: The stomach is made of several kinds of tissue (muscle, gland, nerve) working together, so it is an organ. It belongs to the digestive system, but it is not a whole system by itself. Choosing "a tissue" mixes up one tissue type with the organ that contains several.

screens.title: The major body systems
screens.html:
These systems show up most often on the GED. Learn each one's job.

SystemMain partsMain job
CirculatoryHeart, blood vessels, bloodCarries oxygen, nutrients, hormones, wastes
RespiratoryNose, trachea, lungsBrings in oxygen; removes carbon dioxide
DigestiveEsophagus, stomach, intestines, liverBreaks food down; absorbs nutrients
ExcretoryKidneys, bladderFilters blood; removes liquid waste; balances water
NervousBrain, spinal cord, nervesSenses changes; sends fast signals
EndocrineGlands: pancreas, thyroid, adrenalSends hormones through the blood
ImmuneWhite blood cells, lymph nodesFights pathogens
Muscular / skeletalMuscles, bonesMovement, support, protection
IntegumentarySkin, hair, nailsBarrier; helps control temperature

check.prompt: Sort each organ into its body system.
check.why: The most common mistake is placing the trachea with the digestive organs because it is in the throat. The trachea carries air to the lungs; the esophagus is the tube that carries food to the stomach.
check.hint: Ask what each organ handles: food, air, or liquid waste.
check.explain:
• Digestive: esophagus (carries food to the stomach) and small intestine (absorbs nutrients).
  • Respiratory: trachea (airway) and lungs (gas exchange).
  • Excretory: kidney (filters blood, makes urine) and bladder (stores urine).

screens.title: Systems work together
screens.html:
No system works alone. When you exercise, your respiratory system brings in more oxygen, your circulatory system pumps it faster to your muscles, and your nervous system coordinates it all. After a meal, your digestive system absorbs sugar into the blood, the circulatory system carries it, and the endocrine system releases insulin so cells can take it in.

When a GED question asks which system is most directly responsible, find the exact step the question describes. Loading oxygen into blood is respiratory; delivering it is circulatory.

example.prompt: You touch a hot pan and pull your hand away. Which systems work together?
steps: Receptors in the skin detect the heat, and nerves carry the signal to the spinal cord: nervous system.
The spinal cord sends a signal back to the arm muscles, which pull on the bones: muscular and skeletal systems.
example.answer: The nervous system senses and signals; the muscular and skeletal systems move the hand.

check.prompt: After a meal, nutrients from the small intestine must reach muscle cells in the legs. Which pair of systems is most directly responsible for getting the nutrients there?
options: Digestive and circulatory
Digestive and excretory
Respiratory and circulatory
Nervous and digestive
why: The excretory system removes wastes from the blood; it does not deliver nutrients. The blood vessels of the circulatory system do the delivering.
The respiratory and circulatory pair delivers oxygen. Nutrients come from food, so the digestive system must absorb them first.
Nerves send signals, but they do not carry nutrients. Something must physically transport the nutrients: the blood.
check.hint: One system absorbs the nutrients. Which one carries them through the body?
check.explain: The digestive system breaks food down and absorbs nutrients in the small intestine. The circulatory system then carries them in the blood to the leg muscles. The respiratory and circulatory pair is the oxygen pathway, not the nutrient pathway.

screens.title: Homeostasis
screens.html:
Homeostasis means keeping conditions inside the body stable, even when conditions outside change. Each condition has a set point, a normal value or range:

  • Body temperature: about 37 °C (98.6 °F)
  • Blood glucose (sugar): within a normal range
  • Water and salt balance, blood pH, carbon dioxide level

When something pushes a condition away from its set point, the body detects the change and responds. On a hot day you sweat; on a cold day you shiver. If homeostasis fails, cells cannot work properly, which is why very high fevers or very high blood sugar are dangerous.

options: After a salty meal, a person feels thirsty and drinks water, which restores water balance.
After a salty meal, a person's taste buds report that the food was too salty for him to enjoy.
During a long hike, a person's leg muscles grow larger over the following months of training.
During a cold night, a person chooses to sleep with an extra blanket because she likes the weight.
why: Tasting salt is detecting a flavor, not correcting an internal condition. Nothing here brings an internal level back to normal.
Muscle growth over months is a long-term change, not a correction that returns a condition to its set point.
She chose the blanket because she likes the weight, not because her body detected a change and responded to it.
check.hint: Look for a change inside the body that the body detects and then corrects.
check.explain: Salt raises the concentration of the blood. The body detects it, the brain triggers thirst, and drinking water brings water balance back toward normal. That is homeostasis: detecting a change and correcting it. The other choices describe a taste, a long-term change, and a personal preference.

screens.title: The parts of a feedback loop
screens.html:
The body keeps homeostasis with feedback loops. Every loop has five parts:

Stimulus (the change) → Receptor (detects it) → Control center (compares with the set point and decides; often the brain) → Effector (a muscle, gland, or other organ that acts) → Response (the result)

Clue words help: detect or sense point to the receptor; compares or sends signals point to the control center; the effector is the part that does something, such as sweat glands releasing sweat.

example.prompt: On a hot afternoon, a hiker's temperature rises. Nerve cells in the skin detect it. The hypothalamus in the brain sends signals to sweat glands, which release sweat. As sweat evaporates, the body cools. Label the loop.
steps: Stimulus: body temperature rises. Receptor: nerve cells in the skin.
Control center: the hypothalamus. Effector: sweat glands.
Response: sweat evaporates and the body cools back toward 37 °C.
example.answer: Stimulus: rising temperature; receptor: skin nerve cells; control center: hypothalamus; effector: sweat glands; response: cooling.

check.prompt: Read the description of how the body responds to dehydration. Click the sentence that describes the effector.
spans: After hours of yard work in the heat, Lena's body loses a lot of water in sweat.
Sensors in her brain detect that her blood has become too concentrated.
The brain compares this with the normal level and signals the pituitary gland to release a hormone.
Her kidneys respond to the hormone by returning more water to the blood, so she makes less urine.
Her blood moves back toward its normal water level.
check.why: Many students click the sentence about the brain because it sends the signal, but the brain is the control center. The effector is the organ that carries out the response: the kidneys returning water to the blood.
check.hint: The effector is the organ that actually acts to correct the change.
check.explain: Sentence 1 is the stimulus (water loss), sentence 2 the receptor (sensors detect), sentence 3 the control center (the brain compares and signals), sentence 4 the effector (the kidneys act by saving water), and sentence 5 the response.

screens.title: Negative and positive feedback
screens.html:
Feedback loops come in two types. Compare the direction of the change with the direction of the response.

  • Negative feedback reverses the change and brings the condition back toward normal. Most homeostasis works this way: sweating when hot, shivering when cold, faster breathing when carbon dioxide rises.
  • Positive feedback makes the change grow stronger until an event ends it. Examples: during childbirth, contractions trigger release of the hormone oxytocin, which causes stronger contractions until the baby is born; at a cut, platelets attract more and more platelets until a clot forms.

Negative = "No, go back." Positive = "More, more, more." Negative does not mean bad.

check.prompt: Which of these are examples of positive feedback? Select two answers.
options: Contractions during childbirth trigger release of a hormone that causes even stronger contractions.
Platelets at a cut release chemicals that attract more platelets until the bleeding stops.
When body temperature rises, sweat glands release sweat, and the body cools.
When blood glucose rises, the pancreas releases insulin, and blood glucose falls.
When carbon dioxide builds up in the blood, breathing speeds up and carbon dioxide falls.
why: Temperature goes up and the response brings it down. The response reverses the change, so this is negative feedback.
Glucose goes up and insulin brings it down. Reversing the change is negative feedback, even though insulin itself increases.
Carbon dioxide goes up and faster breathing brings it down. That reversal makes this negative feedback.
check.hint: In positive feedback, the response pushes the same way as the change, and it keeps building.
check.explain: In childbirth, stronger contractions cause even stronger contractions until birth. In clotting, platelets attract more platelets until the cut is sealed. Both build on themselves, so both are positive feedback. Sweating, insulin, and faster breathing each push the condition back toward normal, which is negative feedback.

screens.title: Blood sugar: insulin and glucagon
screens.html:
The pancreas, an endocrine gland, keeps blood glucose in its normal range with two hormones that do opposite jobs:

ConditionHormoneEffect
Glucose too high (after a meal)InsulinCells take in glucose; the liver stores it. Glucose falls.
Glucose too low (between meals)GlucagonThe liver releases stored glucose. Glucose rises.

Both are negative feedback. In diabetes, this system does not work well: in type 1 diabetes the pancreas makes little or no insulin; in type 2 diabetes cells do not respond well to insulin. Either way, blood glucose stays too high.

check.prompt:
Complete the description.

A person skips lunch, and by mid-afternoon her blood glucose has {{0}}. Her pancreas responds by releasing {{1}}, which signals the liver to release stored glucose. This is an example of {{2}} feedback.

options: dropped below normal
risen above normal
stayed exactly the same
why: Skipping a meal means no new glucose is entering the blood while cells keep using it, so the level falls, not rises.
Cells use glucose all the time. With no meal to replace it, the level drops.

options: insulin
glucagon
antibodies
adrenaline
why: Insulin lowers blood glucose. Her glucose is already low, so the pancreas releases the opposite hormone.
Antibodies are immune proteins that attack pathogens; they do not control blood sugar.
Adrenaline comes from the adrenal glands, not the pancreas, and the passage names the pancreas.

options: negative
positive
why: Glucose went down and the response brings it back up. A response that reverses the change is negative feedback, not positive.

check.hint: Which pancreas hormone raises blood glucose? Then compare the change with the response.
check.explain: With no lunch, blood glucose drops below normal. The pancreas releases glucagon, and the liver releases stored glucose, so the level rises back toward normal. The response reverses the change, so it is negative feedback. Insulin is the tempting wrong choice, but insulin lowers glucose.

screens.title: Calories and the 4-4-9 rule
screens.html:
Food gives your body energy, measured in Calories (a food Calorie is a kilocalorie). Three macronutrients supply that energy:

Carbohydrate: 4 Calories per gram
Protein: 4 Calories per gram
Fat: 9 Calories per gram

Vitamins, minerals, and water supply no Calories, but your body still needs them. To find Calories, multiply the grams of each macronutrient by its number, then add.

example.prompt: One serving of a snack has 7 g of fat, 15 g of carbohydrate, and 4 g of protein. How many Calories is that?
steps: Fat: 7 × 9 = 63 Calories.
Carbohydrate: 15 × 4 = 60 Calories. Protein: 4 × 4 = 16 Calories.
Total: 63 + 60 + 16 = 139 Calories.

check.prompt: A sandwich contains 30 g of carbohydrate, 12 g of fat, and 20 g of protein. How many Calories does it contain?

mistakes.why: You used 4 Calories per gram for all three nutrients (62 × 4 = 248). Fat supplies 9 Calories per gram: 12 × 9 = 108.
62 is the total number of grams. Convert each nutrient to Calories first: 30 × 4, 12 × 9, and 20 × 4.
You swapped the numbers for fat and protein (12 × 4 and 20 × 9). Fat is the 9; protein, like carbohydrate, is 4.

check.hint: Use 4 for carbohydrate, 4 for protein, and 9 for fat, then add.
check.explain:
Carbohydrate: 30 × 4 = 120. Fat: 12 × 9 = 108. Protein: 20 × 4 = 80.

Total: 120 + 108 + 80 = 308 Calories.

Using 4 for everything gives 248, which undercounts the fat.

screens.title: Reading a label: servings first
screens.html:
Every number on a Nutrition Facts label is for one serving. Read the label in this order:

  1. Servings per container and serving size.
  2. Figure out how many servings were actually eaten.
  3. Multiply every number you need by that many servings.

If the serving size is given in pieces or cups, divide what was eaten by the serving size to get servings.

example.prompt: Serving size: 3 crackers. Calories per serving: 140. Someone eats 9 crackers. How many Calories?
steps: Servings eaten: 9 ÷ 3 = 3 servings.
Calories: 3 × 140 = 420 Calories.

check.prompt: A bag of pretzels lists: Serving size 1 oz (about 15 pretzels); Servings per container 2.5; Calories 110 per serving. How many Calories are in the whole bag?

mistakes.why: 110 is for one serving. The bag holds 2.5 servings, so multiply: 2.5 × 110.
You multiplied by 2 instead of 2.5. The label says 2.5 servings per container.
You multiplied 110 by 15 pretzels. The 15 pretzels are one serving; multiply by the number of servings, 2.5.

check.hint: Multiply the Calories per serving by the servings per container.
check.explain: Calories in the bag = servings per container × Calories per serving = 2.5 × 110 = 275 Calories.

screens.title: Percent of Calories and % Daily Value
screens.html:
Two different percents appear on nutrition questions:

  • Percent of Calories from a nutrient = (Calories from that nutrient) ÷ (total Calories) × 100. Convert grams to Calories first.
  • % Daily Value (%DV), printed on the label, shows how much of a whole day's recommended amount one serving gives, based on a general 2,000-Calorie diet. 5% or less is low; 20% or more is high.

If someone eats two servings, the %DV doubles too.

example.prompt: A yogurt serving has 150 Calories and 13 g of protein. What percent of its Calories come from protein?
steps: Protein Calories: 13 × 4 = 52.
Percent: 52 ÷ 150 = 0.3466…
≈ 35%.

check.prompt: One serving of a frozen pizza has 300 Calories and 12 g of fat. What percent of the Calories come from fat? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: You divided grams by Calories (12 ÷ 300). Convert fat to Calories first: 12 × 9 = 108.
You used 4 Calories per gram for fat (12 × 4 = 48). Fat supplies 9 Calories per gram.
108 is the number of Calories from fat, not the percent. Divide 108 by the total, 300, then multiply by 100.

check.hint: Fat Calories = grams × 9. Then divide by the total Calories.

screens.title: Energy balance
screens.html:
Your body uses energy all day: to keep your heart beating, your temperature steady, and your muscles moving. Energy balance compares Calories taken in with Calories used.

  • Take in more than you use over time: the extra is stored, mostly as fat, and body mass tends to rise.
  • Take in less than you use: the body draws on stored energy, and body mass tends to fall.
  • About equal: body mass tends to stay about the same.

Physical activity increases the Calories used. A person's needs depend on age, body size, and activity level, which is why the 2,000-Calorie figure on labels is only a general guide.

check.prompt: For several months, a man takes in about 2,600 Calories a day and his body uses about 2,300 Calories a day. If nothing else changes, what is most likely to happen?
options: He will store the extra energy, mostly as fat, and his body mass will tend to rise.
He will burn the extra 300 Calories as heat each day, and his body mass will stay the same.
He will use his stored fat for energy each day, and his body mass will tend to fall.
He will turn the extra Calories into vitamins and minerals, which have no Calories.
why: If the extra energy were all used up, intake would equal use. Here intake is larger, so the extra is stored rather than burned off.
Stored fat is used when intake is less than use. He takes in 300 Calories more than he uses, which is the opposite situation.
Vitamins and minerals come from food; the body does not make them from extra Calories. Extra energy is stored, mostly as fat.
check.hint: Compare intake with use. Which is bigger?
check.explain: Intake (2,600) is greater than use (2,300) by 300 Calories a day. Over time, the body stores the extra energy, mostly as fat, so body mass tends to rise. Using stored fat would happen only if intake were less than use.

screens.title: Infectious and noninfectious disease
screens.html:
Infectious diseases are caused by pathogens (germs) and can spread from one person to another. Noninfectious diseases cannot be caught; they are linked to genes, lifestyle, environment, or aging.

PathogenWhat it isExamples
BacteriaLiving single cells with no nucleusStrep throat, tuberculosis, Lyme disease
VirusNot a cell; copies itself only inside host cellsCold, flu, measles, chickenpox
FungusYeasts and moldsAthlete's foot, ringworm
ParasiteProtists or worms that live on or in a hostMalaria, tapeworm

Noninfectious examples: type 2 diabetes, most heart disease, asthma, scurvy (lack of vitamin C).

check.why: A common mistake is placing scurvy or type 2 diabetes with a pathogen because both make people sick. Neither can be caught from another person: scurvy comes from a lack of vitamin C, and type 2 diabetes is linked to genes and lifestyle.
check.hint: First ask: can you catch it from someone? If yes, which kind of pathogen causes it?
check.explain:
• Bacteria: strep throat.
  • Virus: measles and flu.
  • Fungus: athlete's foot.
  • Noninfectious: type 2 diabetes and scurvy.

screens.title: Antibiotics, viruses, and how disease spreads
screens.html:
Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or stop them from growing by attacking parts that only bacterial cells have, such as the bacterial cell wall. Viruses are not cells and have none of those parts, so antibiotics do not work on viruses. Overusing antibiotics lets resistant bacteria survive and multiply; this is antibiotic resistance.

Pathogens spread in four main ways:

  • Air: droplets from coughs and sneezes (flu, tuberculosis)
  • Direct contact: touching an infected person or surface (athlete's foot)
  • Food or water: contaminated food or drinking water (some food poisoning)
  • Vectors: animals that carry pathogens, such as mosquitoes (malaria) and ticks (Lyme disease)

check.prompt: A doctor tells a patient that her sinus infection is caused by a virus and that antibiotics will not help. Which statement best explains the doctor's reasoning?
options: Antibiotics attack parts of bacterial cells, and a virus is not a cell with those parts.
Antibiotics only work after the body has already made antibodies against that virus.
Viruses are larger than bacteria, so antibiotics cannot get inside a virus to destroy it.
Sinus infections are noninfectious, so no medicine of any kind can affect them at all.
why: This mixes up antibiotics (medicines) with antibodies (made by the body). Antibiotics do not depend on antibodies; they attack bacteria directly.
Viruses are much smaller than bacteria, not larger. Size is not the reason; viruses lack the bacterial structures antibiotics attack.
The infection is caused by a virus, a pathogen, so it is infectious. Being infectious is not the reason antibiotics fail.
check.hint: What do antibiotics attack? Does a virus have it?
check.explain: Antibiotics target structures and processes found in bacterial cells. A virus is not a cell; it copies itself inside the patient's own cells, so the antibiotic has nothing to attack. Confusing antibiotics with antibodies is the most tempting wrong answer.

screens.title: How the body defends itself
screens.html:
The immune system has three lines of defense:

  1. Barriers: skin, mucus, tears, and stomach acid keep most pathogens out.
  2. General defenses: inflammation (redness, swelling), fever, and white blood cells that engulf any invader.
  3. Targeted defenses: white blood cells make antibodies, proteins that fit one specific pathogen and mark it for destruction. Memory cells remain afterward.

Because of memory cells, a second exposure to the same pathogen brings a response that is faster and stronger, often stopping the pathogen before you feel sick. That protection is immunity.

check.prompt: A child gets chickenpox at age 6. At age 30, she is exposed to the chickenpox virus again but does not get sick. What best explains this?
options: Memory cells from the first infection quickly started antibody production against the virus.
Her skin and mucus became thicker as she grew, so the virus could not enter her body.
Antibiotics she took as a child stayed in her blood and destroyed the virus at age 30.
The chickenpox virus can infect only children, so adults are never able to get chickenpox.
why: Barriers block many germs, but they work the same way against every pathogen. Protection against one specific virus comes from memory cells.
Antibiotics do not work on viruses, and they do not stay in the blood for decades.
Adults who were never infected or vaccinated can get chickenpox. Her protection is specific to her, not to her age.
check.hint: What does the first infection leave behind?
check.explain: The first infection left memory cells that recognize the chickenpox virus. At age 30 they triggered fast antibody production, so the virus was stopped before it caused illness. That is immunity.

screens.title: Vaccines and community immunity
screens.html:
A vaccine exposes the immune system to a harmless form or piece of a pathogen. The body makes antibodies and memory cells without having the disease, so a later real infection gets the fast, strong second response.

When most people in a community are immune, a contagious pathogen has trouble finding new people to infect, so it cannot spread easily. This community immunity (herd immunity) also protects people who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborns or people with weak immune systems.

Do not mix these up: antibodies are made by your body. Antibiotics are medicines against bacteria. Vaccines train the immune system ahead of time.

check.prompt: A baby is too young to receive the measles vaccine. Why does living in a town where most people are vaccinated lower the baby's risk of measles?
options: Few people in the town can catch and pass on the virus, so it is less likely to reach the baby.
Vaccinated people release antibodies into the air that protect the unvaccinated people near them.
The vaccine kills measles viruses in the environment, so no virus is left anywhere in the town.
The baby's body makes memory cells from being near other people who have been vaccinated.
why: Antibodies stay inside the vaccinated person's body. They are not released into the air to protect others.
A vaccine trains a person's immune system; it does not destroy viruses in the air, water, or on surfaces.
Memory cells form only when a person's own immune system is exposed to the pathogen or vaccine. Being near vaccinated people does not do that.
check.hint: Think about how a contagious virus travels from person to person.
check.explain: Measles spreads from infected person to person. If most people are immune, the virus cannot pass along a chain of people to reach the baby. That is community immunity. The baby has no memory cells of its own; it is protected by the people around it.

screens.title: Reading health data: rates
screens.html:
Health tables often report disease as a rate instead of a count, so places of different sizes can be compared fairly:

Rate per 100,000 = cases ÷ population × 100,000
Cases = rate × population ÷ 100,000

Other common moves: change = new − old; mean = sum ÷ count; percent change = change ÷ old × 100. Always read the title and units before you calculate.

example.prompt: Town A (60,000 people) had 30 cases. Town B (150,000 people) had 45 cases. Which town had the higher rate?
steps: Town A had fewer cases but the higher rate.

check.prompt: A city of 320,000 people reported 48 cases of tuberculosis last year. What was the rate per 100,000 people?

mistakes.why: That is cases ÷ population. To get a rate per 100,000, multiply by 100,000: 0.00015 × 100,000 = 15.
48 is the number of cases, not the rate. Divide by the population (320,000) and multiply by 100,000.
You multiplied by 10,000 instead of 100,000. The rate is per 100,000 people: 48 ÷ 320,000 × 100,000 = 15.

screens.title: Patterns are not proof
screens.html:
When two things change together, they are correlated. That does not prove one causes the other. A third factor may cause both, or the cause may run the other way.

Example: in one city, months with more ice cream sales also have more drownings. Ice cream does not cause drowning; hot weather increases both ice cream sales and swimming.

To choose the best-supported conclusion on the GED:

  • Describe the pattern for the group that was studied.
  • Reject choices that say proves, always, all, or permanently unless the data truly show that.
  • Reject choices about people, places, or times that were not studied.

check.prompt: A survey of 500 adults in one city found that people who walked at least 30 minutes a day had lower average blood pressure than people who walked less. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: In this group, daily walking was associated with lower average blood pressure.
Walking 30 minutes a day is proven to lower blood pressure in every adult who tries it.
People with low blood pressure walk more because low blood pressure gives them extra energy.
The survey shows that adults in every city should walk 30 minutes a day to stay healthy.
why: A survey shows a pattern; it cannot prove cause, and "every adult" goes far beyond 500 people in one city.
The survey did not measure energy or test which came first. This adds a cause-and-effect story the data do not show.
"Should" is a recommendation, and "every city" goes beyond the one city surveyed. The data describe only this group.
check.hint: Pick the choice that describes the pattern without claiming cause or going beyond the people studied.
check.explain: The survey found that walking and lower blood pressure go together in this group. It did not run an experiment, so it cannot prove that walking caused the lower blood pressure; other factors such as diet or age could play a part. Only the statement that this daily walking was associated with lower blood pressure in this group stays inside the data.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• Organization: cells → tissues → organs → organ systems. Systems work together; the nervous and endocrine systems coordinate them.
  • Homeostasis: stimulus → receptor → control center → effector → response.
  • Negative feedback reverses a change (sweating, shivering, insulin, glucagon). Positive feedback increases it until an event ends it (childbirth, clotting).
  • 4-4-9: carbohydrate 4, protein 4, fat 9 Calories per gram. Multiply label numbers by servings eaten. %DV: 5% low, 20% high.
  • Pathogens: bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites. Antibiotics work on bacteria only.
  • Immunity: antibodies and memory cells; vaccines build them without the disease; community immunity protects others.
  • Data: rate = cases ÷ population × 100,000. Describe the pattern; a pattern is not proof.

Next, go to Practice and start with Set A.

items.prompt: During exercise, the lungs take in extra oxygen. Which body system carries that oxygen from the lungs to the working muscles?
options: Circulatory system
Digestive system
Excretory system
Endocrine system
why: The digestive system breaks down food and absorbs nutrients. It does not carry oxygen; blood does.
The excretory system filters wastes out of the blood. It removes things from the blood rather than delivering oxygen to muscles.
The endocrine system sends hormones, which travel in the blood. The blood itself, part of the circulatory system, carries the oxygen.
items.hint: Which system includes the heart, blood vessels, and blood?
items.explain:
Oxygen enters the blood in the lungs (respiratory system). The circulatory system, made of the heart, blood vessels, and blood, then pumps that oxygen-rich blood to the muscles. This is an example of two systems working together.

The digestive system absorbs nutrients from food, the excretory system filters wastes from the blood, and the endocrine system sends hormones. None of them carries oxygen.

items.prompt: Which volunteer had the lowest resting heart rate?
options: Volunteer A
Volunteer B
Volunteer C
Volunteer D
why: Volunteer A's resting rate is 64 bpm, the second lowest. Volunteer C's rate, 58 bpm, is lower.
Volunteer B's resting rate, 72 bpm, is the highest in the column. You may have looked for the largest value instead of the smallest.
Volunteer D's resting rate is 70 bpm, higher than both A (64) and C (58). Compare all four values before choosing.
items.hint: Look only at the Resting column.
items.explain:
Resting heart rates: A = 64, B = 72, C = 58, D = 70 bpm. The lowest is 58 bpm, Volunteer C.

Volunteer A (64) is the second lowest. Volunteer B has the highest resting rate, so choosing B means reading the column backward.

items.prompt: Sort each body part into the organ system it belongs to.
items.why: The most common mistake is placing the trachea with the digestive system because it is in the throat. The trachea carries air to the lungs; the esophagus is the tube that carries food.
items.hint: Ask what each part does: pumps or carries blood, moves air, handles food, or carries nerve signals.
items.explain:
• Circulatory: heart (pumps blood) and arteries (carry blood away from the heart).
  • Respiratory: lungs (exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide) and trachea (the airway to the lungs).
  • Digestive: small intestine (absorbs nutrients from food).
  • Nervous: spinal cord (carries signals between the brain and the body).

A common mistake is to place the trachea with the digestive system because it is in the throat. The trachea carries air, not food; the esophagus is the food tube.

items.prompt: A person eats the entire package of granola bars. How many Calories does the person consume?
why: 200 is the Calories in one serving (one bar). The package holds 2 servings, so multiply by 2.

100 is half of one serving. The label gives Calories per serving, so for the whole package you multiply, not divide.
items.hint: Check the servings per container. The Calories listed are for one serving.
items.explain:
The label lists 200 Calories per serving and 2 servings per container.

Calories in the whole package = 200 × 2 = 400 Calories.

200 is the amount for just one bar; it ignores the servings per container. 90 comes from doubling the serving weight (45 g), which is grams, not Calories. 100 is half of a serving, not the whole package.

Calories from fat = 8 g × 9 Calories/g = 72 Calories.

A common error is multiplying by 4 (8 × 4 = 32). The value 4 Calories per gram is for carbohydrate and protein; fat supplies 9. Another error is using the %DV (10%) instead of the grams.

58 bpm is Volunteer C's increase (116 − 58), one person's change rather than the change in the mean of all four.
