items.prompt: The passage describes how the body responds to rising temperature. Click the sentence that describes the receptor (sensor) step of the feedback loop.
spans: On a hot afternoon, a hiker's body temperature begins to rise above its normal level of about 37 °C.
Temperature-sensing nerve cells in the skin and in the brain detect the change.
The hypothalamus, a region of the brain, compares this information to the body's normal set point and sends out signals.
Sweat glands in the skin respond by releasing sweat.
As the sweat evaporates, it carries heat away from the body.
The hiker's body temperature moves back toward normal.
items.why: Many students click the hypothalamus sentence because it mentions the brain. The hypothalamus compares and sends signals, so it is the control center; the receptor is the part that detects the change.
items.hint: The receptor is the part that first notices, or detects, the change.
items.explain:
In a feedback loop, the receptor detects the change. Sentence 2 says temperature-sensing nerve cells "detect the change," so it is the receptor step.

  • Sentence 1 is the stimulus (the change itself).
  • Sentence 3 is the control center (the hypothalamus compares to the set point and sends signals).
  • Sentence 4 describes the effector (sweat glands).
  • Sentences 5 and 6 describe the response and its result.

Students often click sentence 3 because it mentions the brain, but the hypothalamus is acting as the control center, not the sensor.

items.prompt: A student has a cold caused by a virus. A friend offers leftover antibiotics. Which statement best explains why antibiotics would not cure the cold?
options: Antibiotics attack structures and processes found in bacteria, and viruses are not cells with those parts.
Antibiotics are designed to work only against fungi, and colds are caused by viruses instead of fungi.
Viruses are much larger than bacteria, so antibiotic molecules cannot surround and destroy them.
A cold is a noninfectious disease, so it cannot be treated by any kind of medicine at all.
why: Antibiotics are made to fight bacteria, not fungi. Fungal infections are treated with different medicines called antifungals.
Viruses are much smaller than bacteria, not larger. The real reason is that viruses lack the bacterial structures antibiotics attack.
A cold is infectious: a virus causes it and it spreads from person to person. Being infectious is not why antibiotics fail.
items.hint: Think about what kind of pathogen antibiotics are designed to kill and whether a virus is a living cell.
items.explain:
Antibiotics target parts and processes of bacterial cells, such as the bacterial cell wall. A virus is not a cell; it reproduces only inside the host's own cells and has none of those bacterial parts, so antibiotics have nothing to attack.

Antibiotics are designed for bacteria, not fungi. Viruses are much smaller than bacteria, not larger. A cold is infectious: it is caused by a pathogen and spreads from person to person.

items.prompt:
Complete the description of Person 1's results.

During the first 30 minutes after the drink, Person 1's blood glucose {{0}}. The pancreas responded by releasing the hormone {{1}}, which signals body cells to take in glucose from the blood. By 120 minutes, Person 1's level had {{2}}. Because this response {{3}} the original change, it is an example of negative feedback.

options: rose
fell
stayed the same
why: The level went from 88 to 150 mg/dL in the first 30 minutes, which is an increase, not a decrease.
The level changed from 88 to 150 mg/dL, so it did not stay the same.

options: insulin
glucagon
adrenaline
antibodies
why: Glucagon raises blood glucose when it is too low. Here glucose was high, so the pancreas released the hormone that lowers it.
Adrenaline comes from the adrenal glands, not the pancreas, and it does not signal cells to take in glucose.
Antibodies are immune proteins that attack pathogens; they are not hormones.

options: returned close to its starting value
kept rising above its 30-minute value
fallen far below the normal range
why: After 30 minutes the level fell: 150, 135, 115, 98. It did not keep rising.
At 120 minutes the level was 98 mg/dL, which is within the normal range of about 70–99, not far below it.

options: reverses
increases
has no effect on
why: If the response increased the change, glucose would keep climbing, which would be positive feedback. Person 1's glucose came back down.
The level fell from 150 back to 98 mg/dL, so the response clearly had an effect.

items.hint: Read Person 1's row from left to right. Which pancreas hormone lowers blood glucose?
items.explain:
1. Person 1's glucose went from 88 to 150 mg/dL, so it rose.
  2. The pancreas releases insulin, which signals cells to take in glucose. Glucagon does the opposite: it raises glucose when it is too low.
  3. By 120 minutes the level was 98 mg/dL, close to the starting 88, so it had returned close to its starting value.
  4. The response brought glucose down after it went up, so it reverses the change. That is what makes it negative feedback.

items.prompt: Which of the following are examples of negative feedback? Select three answers.
options: A person shivers when body temperature drops, and the heat produced warms the body.
During childbirth, contractions trigger the release of a hormone that causes even stronger contractions.
When the body is low on water, the kidneys make less urine, which helps conserve water.
At a cut, platelets release chemicals that attract more and more platelets until a clot forms.
When blood glucose drops too low, the pancreas releases glucagon, and blood glucose rises.
why: Each contraction leads to an even stronger one. The response builds on the change until the baby is born, which is positive feedback.
Platelets attract more platelets, so the response builds on itself until the clot forms. That is positive feedback.
items.hint: For each one, ask: does the response push the condition back toward normal, or make the change bigger?
items.explain:
Negative feedback reverses a change:

  • Shivering: temperature falls → heat is produced → temperature rises back. Reverses the change.
  • Kidneys: water is low → less water is lost in urine → water levels are restored. Reverses the change.
  • Glucagon: glucose is low → glucagon causes glucose release → glucose rises back. Reverses the change.

Positive feedback makes a change bigger until an event ends it: childbirth contractions grow stronger until birth, and platelets attract more platelets until the clot forms. These two are the distractors.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data in the table?
options: Among these four volunteers, the one with the lowest resting heart rate was also the closest to his or her resting rate 3 minutes after jogging.
Jogging in place for a few minutes every day for a year will permanently lower a person's resting heart rate by several beats per minute.
Every volunteer's heart rate increased by exactly the same number of beats per minute from resting to immediately after jogging.
All healthy adults return to their exact resting heart rate within 3 minutes after they stop jogging in place for 4 minutes.
why: The study measured one short jog, not daily jogging over a year. Long-term effects were never tested, so this goes beyond the data.
The increases were A: 64, B: 68, C: 58, and D: 66 bpm. They are close but not the same.
No volunteer was back to the exact resting rate at 3 minutes (for example, A was 70 versus 64), and four volunteers cannot represent all adults.
items.hint: For each volunteer, subtract the resting rate from the 3-minutes-after rate. Then check whether each choice stays within what was measured.
items.explain:
Difference between 3 minutes after and resting:

  • A: 70 − 64 = 6
  • B: 80 − 72 = 8
  • C: 62 − 58 = 4
  • D: 76 − 70 = 6

Volunteer C has the lowest resting rate (58) and the smallest difference (4), so the statement about the volunteer with the lowest resting rate is supported for these four volunteers.

The study did not test daily jogging or long-term effects, so the "permanently lower" claim goes beyond the data. Increases during jogging were A: 64, B: 68, C: 58, D: 66, which are not the same. No volunteer was back to the exact resting rate after 3 minutes, and four volunteers cannot represent all adults.

items.prompt: Which statement is best supported by the data in the table?
options: As the percent of vaccinated kindergarten children decreased, the reported cases per 100,000 people increased.
The vaccine itself caused the yearly increase in reported cases of the disease in this county.
The number of reported cases per 100,000 people doubled every single year from 2016 to 2020.
Any county with a vaccination rate below 90% will have more than 3 cases per 100,000 people.
why: Cases rose as fewer children were vaccinated. If the vaccine caused the disease, cases would rise as vaccination rose, which is the opposite of the data.
From 2016 to 2017, the rate went from 0.4 to 0.5, an increase of only 0.1, not a doubling.
The data come from one county only. A rule about "any county" goes beyond the data.
items.hint: Describe the trend in each column. Then reject any answer that claims more than the table shows.
items.explain:
Reading the table: the vaccination rate fell every year (95 → 94 → 91 → 88 → 85%), and reported cases rose every year (0.4 → 0.5 → 1.2 → 3.8 → 9.6 per 100,000). So the statement that cases rose as vaccination fell accurately describes the pattern. This pattern fits the idea of community immunity: when fewer people are immune, a contagious pathogen spreads more easily.

The vaccine could not have caused the increase, because cases rose as fewer children were vaccinated. Cases did not double every year: 0.4 to 0.5 is an increase of only 0.1. The statement about "any county" goes beyond the data, because the data come from one county only.

items.prompt: What percent of the Calories in one granola bar come from carbohydrate? Use 4 Calories per gram of carbohydrate and the label's total of 200 Calories. Enter a number.

mistakes.why: You divided grams by Calories (27 ÷ 200). Convert carbohydrate to Calories first: 27 × 4 = 108.
10% is the % Daily Value for carbohydrate, which compares to a whole day's diet. This question asks what share of the bar's own Calories come from carbohydrate.
108 is the number of Calories from carbohydrate. To get the percent, divide by 200 and multiply by 100.

items.hint: Carbohydrate Calories = grams × 4. Then divide by the total Calories and multiply by 100.
items.explain:
Carbohydrate Calories: 27 g × 4 = 108 Calories.

Percent: 108 ÷ 200 = 0.54 = 54%.

Check: fat 8 × 9 = 72 (36%), protein 5 × 4 = 20 (10%), and 54% + 36% + 10% = 100%. Using the %DV (10%) is the most tempting wrong answer, but %DV compares with a daily diet, not with the bar's Calories.

items.prompt: At 120 minutes, Person 2's blood glucose was still 220 mg/dL, while Person 1's was 98 mg/dL. Which explanation is best supported by the information?
options: Person 2's cells do not respond normally to insulin, so glucose is not moved out of the blood efficiently.
Person 2's pancreas released extra insulin, and insulin is the hormone that raises blood glucose levels.
Person 2 drank a larger glucose drink than Person 1, so much more glucose entered the blood after it.
Person 2's high glucose started positive feedback that made the stomach digest more and more glucose.
why: Insulin lowers blood glucose by signaling cells to take it in. Glucagon is the hormone that raises it.
The passage says both people drank the same drink with 75 g of glucose, so the amount of glucose was controlled.
The stomach does not make glucose in response to high blood glucose, and the passage describes no such loop. The problem is that the normal negative feedback is not working well.
items.hint: Reread how the passage describes type 2 diabetes. What does insulin normally do?
items.explain:
Normally, rising glucose causes the pancreas to release insulin, and insulin signals cells to take in glucose, so the level falls (negative feedback). Person 1 shows this: 150 → 98 mg/dL. The passage says Person 2 has type 2 diabetes, in which cells do not respond normally to insulin, so glucose stays high: 245 → 220 mg/dL.

The amount of glucose was the same for both people, and insulin lowers glucose rather than raising it.

items.prompt: In 2020, the county had a population of 500,000 people. Use the table to find how many cases of the disease were reported in the county in 2020.

mistakes.why: 9.6 is the rate per 100,000 people, not the number of cases. The county has 500,000 people, which is 5 groups of 100,000: 9.6 × 5 = 48.
You multiplied the rate by the whole population (9.6 × 500,000) and forgot to divide by 100,000. Cases = 9.6 × 500,000 ÷ 100,000 = 48.
You divided by 10,000 instead of 100,000. The rate is per 100,000 people: 9.6 × 500,000 ÷ 100,000 = 48.

items.hint: The rate is per 100,000 people. How many groups of 100,000 live in the county?
items.explain:
Rate in 2020: 9.6 cases per 100,000 people.

Groups of 100,000: 500,000 ÷ 100,000 = 5.

Cases: 9.6 × 5 = 48 cases.

The most common error is to report 9.6, the rate, as the number of cases.

items.prompt: Which body system filters wastes such as urea out of the blood and removes them from the body in urine?
options: Excretory system
Digestive system
Respiratory system
Circulatory system
why: The digestive system removes undigested food as solid waste. It does not filter the blood or make urine.
The respiratory system removes one waste, carbon dioxide, by breathing it out. Urine is made by the kidneys.
The circulatory system carries wastes to the kidneys, but it does not filter them out. The kidneys of the excretory system do the filtering.
items.hint: Which system includes the kidneys and bladder?
items.explain: The excretory system (kidneys and bladder) filters wastes such as urea from the blood and removes them in urine. The circulatory system delivers blood to the kidneys, which is the most tempting wrong answer, but the filtering happens in the kidneys.

items.prompt: Which volunteer had the highest breathing rate immediately after climbing the stairs?
options: Volunteer W
Volunteer X
Volunteer Y
Volunteer Z
why: Volunteer W's rate immediately after climbing was 32 breaths per minute. Y's rate, 38, is higher.
Volunteer X's rate, 28 breaths per minute, is the lowest in that column. You may have looked for the smallest value.
Volunteer Z's rate immediately after climbing was 30 breaths per minute, lower than Y's 38.
items.hint: Use only the Immediately after climbing column.
items.explain: Immediately after climbing: W = 32, X = 28, Y = 38, Z = 30 breaths per minute. The highest is 38, Volunteer Y. Volunteer Y also had the highest resting rate, but the question asks only about the column right after climbing.

items.prompt: Sort each body part into the organ system it belongs to.
items.why: The most common mistake is putting the thyroid or adrenal glands in the nervous system because they help control the body. They control it by releasing hormones into the blood, which makes them endocrine glands.
items.hint: Ask: does it send electrical signals, release hormones, or fight pathogens?
items.explain:
• Nervous: brain and nerves send fast electrical signals.
  • Endocrine: the thyroid gland and adrenal glands release hormones into the blood.
  • Immune: lymph nodes filter pathogens, and white blood cells attack them.

items.prompt: A person eats the entire can of soup. How many Calories does the person consume?
why: 90 is the Calories in one serving (1 cup). The can holds about 2.5 servings.
180 is 2 servings × 90. The label says about 2.5 servings per container, not 2.
36 is 90 ÷ 2.5. Eating more than one serving means you multiply by the servings, not divide.
items.hint: Every number on the label is for one serving. How many servings are in the can?
items.explain:
Calories per serving = 90. Servings per container = 2.5.

90 × 2.5 = 225 Calories.

Choosing 90 ignores the servings per container, and 180 rounds 2.5 servings down to 2.

items.prompt: Carbohydrate supplies 4 Calories per gram. How many Calories in one serving of the soup come from carbohydrate?

mistakes.why: You multiplied by 9 (12 × 9). Nine Calories per gram is for fat; carbohydrate supplies 4: 12 × 4 = 48.
120 is the carbohydrate Calories in the whole can (2.5 servings × 48). The question asks for one serving.
You multiplied by 4 but used 4% (the % Daily Value) as if it were grams. Use the 12 g of total carbohydrate.

items.hint: Find the grams of total carbohydrate in one serving and multiply by 4.
items.explain:
Total carbohydrate in one serving = 12 g.

Calories from carbohydrate = 12 × 4 = 48 Calories.

Using 9 Calories per gram (the fat value) gives 108, which is more than the whole serving's 90 Calories, a sign that something went wrong.

items.prompt: The mean resting breathing rate of the four volunteers was 14 breaths per minute. What was the increase in the mean breathing rate from resting to immediately after climbing?
options: 18 breaths per minute
32 breaths per minute
26 breaths per minute
22 breaths per minute
why: 32 is the mean breathing rate immediately after climbing. The increase is that mean minus the resting mean: 32 − 14.
26 is the highest value in the table minus the lowest (38 − 12). Those values belong to different volunteers and different times.
22 is Volunteer Y's increase (38 − 16), one person's change rather than the change in the mean.
items.hint: Find the mean of the Immediately after climbing column, then subtract 14.
items.explain:
Mean immediately after climbing = (32 + 28 + 38 + 30) ÷ 4 = 128 ÷ 4 = 32 breaths per minute.

Resting mean = (14 + 12 + 16 + 14) ÷ 4 = 56 ÷ 4 = 14.

Increase = 32 − 14 = 18 breaths per minute.

32 is the mean after climbing, not the increase, and 22 is only Volunteer Y's increase.

items.prompt: The passage describes how the body responds when a person stands up quickly. Click the sentence that describes the control center of the feedback loop.
spans: When a person stands up quickly from lying down, blood pressure in the upper body drops for a moment.
Pressure sensors in the walls of large arteries in the neck detect the drop.
The brainstem compares these signals with the normal blood pressure and sends nerve signals to the heart.
The heart responds by beating faster and harder.
Within seconds, blood pressure rises back to its normal level.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the sentence about the pressure sensors, because it is the first sentence that mentions the body reacting. Those sensors only detect the drop; the brainstem compares it with the normal level and decides, which makes it the control center.
items.hint: The control center compares the change with the normal level and sends out instructions.
items.explain: Sentence 1 is the stimulus (blood pressure drops). Sentence 2 is the receptor (pressure sensors detect it). Sentence 3 is the control center: the brainstem compares the signals with the normal level and sends signals out. Sentence 4 is the effector (the heart), and sentence 5 is the response. This is negative feedback, because the response raises the pressure back after it fell.

items.prompt: Lab tests show that the pathogen causing a patient's illness is not made of cells and can make copies of itself only inside the patient's own cells. Which conclusion is correct?
options: The pathogen is a virus, so an antibiotic will not destroy it.
The pathogen is a bacterium, so an antibiotic will destroy it.
The pathogen is a fungus, so it can spread only through touch.
The pathogen is a parasite, so it must be carried by a mosquito.
why: Bacteria are living cells that reproduce on their own. A pathogen that is not made of cells cannot be a bacterium.
Fungi are made of cells, such as yeast cells or mold threads. The lab found no cells, which rules out a fungus.
Parasites such as protists and worms are made of cells, and not all of them use mosquitoes. A pathogen with no cells is a virus.
items.hint: Which kind of pathogen is not a cell and must use a host cell to reproduce?
items.explain: Only a virus is not made of cells and reproduces only inside host cells. Bacteria, fungi, and parasites are all made of cells. Because antibiotics attack parts of bacterial cells, an antibiotic will not destroy a virus.

items.prompt:
Complete the description of temperature control during the run.

As the runners ran, their core body temperature {{0}}. Temperature receptors detected the change, and the hypothalamus sent signals to the sweat glands, which acted as the {{1}} in this loop. As sweat {{2}}, it carried heat away from the body. Because this response opposes the change in temperature, it is an example of {{3}} feedback.

options: rose
fell
stayed the same
why: In both trials, core temperature went up from 37.0 °C, so it did not fall.
Core temperature changed in both trials, from 37.0 °C to 38.5 or 39.3 °C.

options: effectors
receptors
control center
why: The receptors are the temperature sensors that detected the change. The sweat glands carry out the response.
The hypothalamus is the control center; it sent the signals. The sweat glands act on those signals.

options: evaporated from the skin
was absorbed back into the blood
was stored in the kidneys
why: Sweat cools the body by leaving it. Sweat that went back into the blood would carry no heat away.
The kidneys filter blood and make urine; they do not store sweat. Cooling happens at the skin.

options: negative
positive
why: Positive feedback would push temperature even higher. Sweating opposes the rise, which is negative feedback.

items.hint: Which part of a feedback loop carries out the response? How does sweat remove heat?
items.explain:
1. In both trials, core temperature rose from 37.0 °C.
  2. The sweat glands carried out the response, so they were the effectors; the hypothalamus was the control center.
  3. Sweat removes heat when it evaporates from the skin.
  4. The response works against the rise in temperature, so it is negative feedback.

items.prompt: Which of the following are examples of negative feedback? Select three answers.
options: After a person stands up quickly and blood pressure drops, the heart beats faster and blood pressure rises.
While a baby nurses, a hormone is released that lets milk flow, so the baby keeps nursing and more hormone is released.
On a hot day, blood vessels in the skin widen, so more heat leaves the body and temperature falls.
When a blood vessel is torn, each activated clotting protein activates more clotting proteins until a clot forms.
After a person drinks a large amount of water, the kidneys make more urine, and extra water leaves the body.
why: Nursing causes hormone release, which leads to more nursing and more hormone. The response strengthens the original change, so this is positive feedback.
Each clotting protein activates more of them, so the process builds on itself until the clot forms. That is positive feedback.
items.hint: Draw two arrows for each: the change and the response. Opposite directions mean negative feedback.
items.explain:
Negative feedback reverses a change:

  • Blood pressure drops → the heart works harder → blood pressure rises back.
  • Temperature rises → skin vessels widen and release heat → temperature falls back.
  • Too much water → kidneys make more urine → water level falls back.

Nursing and clotting are positive feedback: in each, the response makes the process stronger until an event (the baby stops nursing, the clot forms) ends it.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: The mean breathing rate dropped more in the first 2 minutes after climbing than in the next 2 minutes.
Every volunteer's breathing rate was back to his or her exact resting rate within 2 minutes after climbing.
The volunteers with higher resting breathing rates breathed more slowly than the others right after climbing.
Climbing five flights of stairs each day causes a lasting increase in a person's resting breathing rate.
why: At 2 minutes, every rate was still above resting (for example, W was 22 versus 14). Even at 4 minutes, only some were close.
Volunteer Y had the highest resting rate (16) and also the highest rate after climbing (38), which is the opposite of this claim.
The class measured one climb, not daily climbing, and did not measure resting rates on later days. A lasting effect was never tested.
items.hint: Find the mean at each time. Then compare the drop from 0 to 2 minutes with the drop from 2 to 4 minutes.
items.explain:
Means: resting 14, immediately after 32, 2 minutes after (22 + 18 + 26 + 22) ÷ 4 = 88 ÷ 4 = 22, 4 minutes after (16 + 13 + 19 + 16) ÷ 4 = 64 ÷ 4 = 16.

Drop in the first 2 minutes: 32 − 22 = 10. Drop in the next 2 minutes: 22 − 16 = 6. So the mean dropped more in the first 2 minutes than in the next 2, and that statement is supported.

No one was back to resting at 2 minutes, Y breathed fastest of all after climbing, and the study never tested daily climbing.

items.prompt: Which statement is best supported by the data in the table?
options: After the program began, both the mosquitoes caught per trap and the case rate went down each year.
The program proves that clearing standing water completely removes this disease from a county.
The reported case rate fell by about half every year from the start of 2018 to the end of 2022.
Clearing standing water lowered the case rate because the virus is spread in drinking water.
why: In 2022 the rate was still 1.2 cases per 100,000, so the disease was not removed. Data from one county also cannot prove a rule for all counties.
From 2018 to 2019 the rate went up, from 6.0 to 6.4. It did not fall by half every year.
The passage says the virus is spread by mosquito bites. Standing water matters because mosquitoes lay their eggs in it, not because people drink it.
items.hint: Check each column from 2020 to 2022. Then reject any choice that claims more than the table shows or contradicts the passage.
items.explain:
From 2019 to 2022, mosquitoes caught per trap fell 45 → 30 → 18 → 11, and the case rate fell 6.4 → 4.1 → 2.2 → 1.2. The statement that both values went down each year after the program began describes this pattern. It fits the idea of a vector: fewer mosquitoes means fewer chances for the virus to reach people.

The disease was not eliminated (1.2 in 2022), the rate rose from 2018 to 2019, and the passage says the virus spreads through mosquito bites, not water.

items.prompt: What percent of the Calories in one serving of the soup come from fat? Use 9 Calories per gram of fat and the label's total of 90 Calories. Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 3% is the % Daily Value for fat, which compares to a whole day's diet. This question asks what share of the soup's own Calories come from fat.
You used 4 Calories per gram for fat (2 × 4 = 8, and 8 ÷ 90 ≈ 8.9%). Fat supplies 9 Calories per gram: 2 × 9 = 18.
18 is the number of Calories from fat. To get the percent, divide by 90 and multiply by 100.

items.hint: Fat Calories = grams × 9. Then divide by the total Calories and multiply by 100.
items.explain:
Fat Calories: 2 g × 9 = 18 Calories.

Percent: 18 ÷ 90 = 0.20 = 20%.

Check: carbohydrate 12 × 4 = 48 and protein 6 × 4 = 24; 18 + 48 + 24 = 90, which matches the label. The %DV for fat (3%) is a different percent: it compares with a whole day's fat.

items.prompt: At 60 minutes, the runners' mean core temperature was 0.8 °C higher in the no-water trial than in the water trial. Which explanation is best supported by the data?
options: Without water, the runners lost more body water and made less sweat, so less heat was removed by evaporation.
In the no-water trial, the runners ran at a faster pace than in the water trial, so their muscles made more heat.
In the no-water trial, the runners made more sweat than in the water trial, and sweating raises core temperature.
Without water, the hypothalamus stopped working, so the body had no control center to regulate its temperature.
why: The passage says both runs were at the same pace, so pace was controlled and cannot explain the difference.
The table shows less sweat without water (1.3 L versus 1.5 L), and sweating lowers body temperature as it evaporates.
Sweating still occurred in the no-water trial (1.3 L), and the hypothalamus is what signals the sweat glands, so the control center was still working. Nothing in the data shows it stopped.
items.hint: Compare the body mass lost and the sweat produced in the two trials. How does sweat cool the body?
items.explain:
In the no-water trial the runners lost more body mass (1.4 kg versus 0.4 kg), which is mostly water, and produced less sweat (1.3 L versus 1.5 L). Less sweat means less evaporation and less heat carried away, so core temperature climbed higher: 39.3 °C versus 38.5 °C (39.3 − 38.5 = 0.8). Sweat is made from water in the blood, so a runner who does not replace lost water has less to sweat with.

Pace was the same in both trials, and the data show less sweat, not more, without water.

items.prompt: The county had a population of 250,000 people in 2019. Use the table to find how many cases of the disease were reported in the county in 2019.

mistakes.why: 6.4 is the rate per 100,000 people, not the number of cases. The county has 2.5 groups of 100,000: 6.4 × 2.5 = 16.
You multiplied the rate by the whole population and forgot to divide by 100,000. Cases = 6.4 × 250,000 ÷ 100,000 = 16.
15 comes from the 2018 rate (6.0 × 2.5). The question asks about 2019, when the rate was 6.4.

items.hint: The rate is per 100,000 people. How many groups of 100,000 live in the county?
items.explain:
Rate in 2019: 6.4 cases per 100,000 people.

Groups of 100,000: 250,000 ÷ 100,000 = 2.5.

Cases: 6.4 × 2.5 = 16 cases.

Reporting 6.4, the rate itself, is the most common error.

items.prompt: Emphysema is a lung disease that damages the tiny air sacs (alveoli) where oxygen passes into the blood. Which effect on another body system is most likely?
options: Muscle cells receive less oxygen, so the person tires more quickly during activity.
The small intestine absorbs fewer nutrients, so the person slowly loses body mass.
The kidneys filter more blood than usual, so the person makes much more urine.
The skin releases more sweat than usual, so the person's body cools down faster.
why: Nutrients are absorbed by the digestive system, which emphysema does not damage. The alveoli handle oxygen, not food.
Nothing in emphysema makes the kidneys filter more. The direct link from the alveoli is to the oxygen the blood carries to cells.
Sweating is controlled by temperature, not by lung damage. The alveoli connect to the circulatory system through oxygen.
items.explain: Damaged alveoli let less oxygen into the blood. The circulatory system then delivers less oxygen to cells, so muscle cells cannot make as much ATP through cellular respiration, and the person tires quickly. This chain (respiratory → circulatory → muscular) shows systems depending on one another. The other choices link the lungs to systems that do not depend on the alveoli.

items.prompt:
Read the description, then complete the statement.

At high altitude, the air holds less oxygen, so blood oxygen falls. Cells in the kidneys detect the low oxygen and release a hormone called EPO. EPO signals the bone marrow to make more red blood cells. With more red blood cells, the blood carries more oxygen, and blood oxygen rises toward normal.

In this loop, the kidney cells that detect the low oxygen act as the {{0}}, and the bone marrow acts as the {{1}}. The loop is {{2}} feedback.

options: receptor
effector
stimulus
why: The effector carries out the response. The kidney cells detect the change; the bone marrow is the part that makes the new red blood cells.
The stimulus is the change itself, the drop in blood oxygen. The kidney cells are body parts that detect that change.

options: effector
receptor
control center
why: The bone marrow does not detect low oxygen; the kidney cells do. The bone marrow responds by making red blood cells.
The bone marrow does not compare levels or send signals. It receives the EPO signal and carries out the response.

options: negative
positive
why: Blood oxygen fell and the response raises it back toward normal. A response that reverses the change is negative, not positive, feedback.

items.explain: The kidney cells detect the low oxygen, so they are the receptor (here they also release the hormone). The bone marrow carries out the response by making red blood cells, so it is the effector. Oxygen fell and the response brings it back up, so this is negative feedback.

items.prompt: Which situation is an example of positive feedback?
options: During labor, contractions trigger release of oxytocin, which causes even stronger contractions.
After a meal, rising blood glucose triggers insulin release, and blood glucose falls back to normal.
In a cold room, falling body temperature triggers shivering, and body temperature rises to normal.
During a run, rising carbon dioxide triggers faster breathing, and carbon dioxide falls to normal.
why: Glucose rose and insulin brought it back down. The response reverses the change, which is negative feedback.
Temperature fell and shivering brought it back up. Reversing the change makes this negative feedback.
Carbon dioxide rose and faster breathing brought it back down. That reversal is negative feedback.
items.explain: In labor, contractions cause oxytocin release, which causes stronger contractions, which cause more oxytocin. The response builds on the change until the baby is born, so it is positive feedback. In each of the other choices, the response returns the condition to normal, which is negative feedback.

items.prompt: Fat supplies 9 Calories per gram. How many Calories in one serving of the macaroni and cheese come from fat?

mistakes.why: You multiplied by 4 (14 × 4). Fat supplies 9 Calories per gram: 14 × 9 = 126.
18 is the % Daily Value for fat, not Calories. Multiply the 14 g of fat by 9.
252 is the fat Calories for the whole package (2 servings). The question asks for one serving.

items.explain: Total fat in one serving = 14 g. Calories from fat = 14 × 9 = 126 Calories. Using 4 Calories per gram (the value for carbohydrate and protein) gives 56, which is the most common error.

items.prompt: A person eats the whole package of macaroni and cheese. Which statement about the sodium the person consumes is correct?
options: It is 80% of the Daily Value, so it is high in sodium.
It is 40% of the Daily Value, so it is high in sodium.
It is 20% of the Daily Value, so it is moderate in sodium.
It is 80% of the Daily Value, so it is low because it is under 100%.
why: 40% is the sodium in one serving. The package holds 2 servings, so the person gets 2 × 40% = 80%.
You divided 40% between the two servings. Eating both servings means multiplying: 2 × 40% = 80%.
The 80% is right, but %DV is not judged against 100%. Any value of 20% or more is high.
items.explain: One serving has 40% DV of sodium, and the package holds 2 servings: 2 × 40% = 80% DV. Because 80% is well above 20%, the amount is high. Forgetting to multiply by the servings (40%) is the most tempting wrong answer.

items.prompt: A patient has strep throat, an infection caused by bacteria. Which statements are correct? Select two answers.
options: An antibiotic may be used to treat it, because the pathogen is a living cell.
The patient's white blood cells can make antibodies that target this specific bacterium.
An antibiotic taken now will also protect the patient from catching the flu next month.
Strep throat is noninfectious, so the patient cannot pass it to family members.
The patient's own body will make antibiotics that destroy the bacteria in the throat.
why: Flu is caused by a virus, and antibiotics do not work on viruses. Antibiotics also do not give lasting protection the way memory cells do.
Strep throat is caused by a pathogen, so it is infectious and can spread, for example through droplets from coughs.
This confuses antibiotics with antibodies. The body makes antibodies; antibiotics are medicines.
items.explain: Bacteria are living cells, so antibiotics can attack them. The immune system also responds with antibodies made for this specific bacterium. Antibiotics do not protect against the flu virus, strep throat is infectious, and the body makes antibodies, not antibiotics.

items.prompt: How many times as high was the peak antibody level after the second dose as the peak antibody level after the first dose?

mistakes.why: 320 is the difference between the peaks (360 − 40). "How many times as high" asks you to divide: 360 ÷ 40 = 9.
You divided 360 by 20, but 20 is not the first-dose peak. The first dose peaked at 40 AU on day 14.

items.explain:
First-dose peak: 40 AU (day 14). Second-dose peak: 360 AU (day 14).

360 ÷ 40 = 9 times as high.

Subtracting (360 − 40 = 320) finds how much higher, not how many times as high.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data and the passage?
options: The second dose produced a faster and larger antibody response than the first dose.
The first dose produced no antibodies, so only the second dose gave any protection.
After the second dose, antibody levels stayed at their peak for the rest of the study.
The second response was larger because the second dose contained more vaccine.
why: After the first dose, antibodies rose to 40 AU, so the first dose did produce antibodies. It also left memory cells that made the second response possible.
The level fell from 360 AU on day 14 to 300 AU on day 28, so it did not stay at its peak.
The passage says the two doses were identical. The larger response comes from memory cells made after the first dose.
items.explain: On day 7, the level was 6 AU after the first dose but 240 AU after the second, so the second response was faster. Its peak (360 AU) was 9 times the first peak (40 AU), so it was larger. Memory cells from the first dose explain this. The doses were identical, the first dose did make antibodies, and the level after the second dose declined from its peak.

items.prompt: Celiac disease damages the lining of the small intestine, where nutrients pass into the blood. Which effect on the rest of the body is most likely?
options: Fewer nutrients enter the blood, so body cells may lack energy and building materials.
Less oxygen enters the blood from the lungs, so the person's breathing slows down.
The kidneys stop filtering the blood, so wastes build up and no urine is produced.
Nerve signals travel more slowly, because the spinal cord is not able to absorb food.
why: Oxygen enters the blood in the lungs, not the small intestine. Celiac disease affects nutrient absorption.
Celiac disease affects the small intestine, not the kidneys. Nothing in the description links it to kidney filtering.
The spinal cord carries nerve signals; it never absorbs food. Nutrients are absorbed by the small intestine.
items.explain: The small intestine (digestive system) absorbs nutrients into the blood, and the circulatory system carries them to every cell. If the lining is damaged, fewer nutrients reach the blood, so cells may not get enough glucose for energy or materials for growth and repair. The other choices connect the intestine to jobs done by the lungs, kidneys, or nerves.

items.prompt:
Read the description, then complete the statement.

After a very salty meal, the blood becomes too concentrated. Sensor cells in the brain detect the change. The hypothalamus compares the level with the normal set point and triggers the feeling of thirst. The person drinks water, and the blood becomes less concentrated.

In this loop, the sensor cells act as the {{0}}, and the hypothalamus acts as the {{1}}. The loop is {{2}} feedback.

options: receptor
effector
stimulus
why: The effector carries out the response. The sensor cells only detect the change.
The stimulus is the change itself, the blood becoming too concentrated. The sensor cells are what detect it.

options: control center
receptor
effector
why: The sensor cells are the receptor. The hypothalamus compares the level with the set point and triggers the response.
The hypothalamus does not drink the water; it decides that a response is needed. Comparing and deciding is the control center's job.

options: negative
positive
why: The blood became more concentrated, and drinking water made it less concentrated. That reversal is negative feedback.

items.explain: The sensor cells detect the change, so they are the receptor. The hypothalamus compares with the set point and triggers thirst, so it is the control center. The response (drinking) brings the blood back toward normal, so this is negative feedback.

items.prompt: A student says, "Negative feedback is harmful because it makes conditions in the body worse." Which response best corrects the student?
options: Negative feedback reverses a change and returns conditions toward normal, so it usually keeps the body healthy.
Negative feedback increases a change until an event ends it, such as the birth of a baby during labor.
Negative feedback happens only when the body is already sick, such as when a person has a high fever.
Negative feedback is controlled only by hormones and never involves the nervous system or the brain.
why: This describes positive feedback. Childbirth contractions grow stronger until birth; negative feedback does the opposite and reverses a change.
Negative feedback works all day in healthy people, for example when you sweat on a warm day or when insulin lowers glucose after a meal.
Many negative feedback loops use the nervous system, such as the hypothalamus controlling sweating and shivering.
items.explain: "Negative" describes direction, not harm: the response goes the opposite way from the change, so conditions return toward normal. That is how most homeostasis works, which makes negative feedback essential to health. The tempting wrong answer describes positive feedback.

items.prompt: Fat supplies 9 Calories per gram. How many Calories in one serving of the peanut butter come from fat?

mistakes.why: You multiplied by 4 (16 × 4). Fat supplies 9 Calories per gram: 16 × 9 = 144.
21 is the % Daily Value for fat, not Calories. Multiply the 16 g of fat by 9.
You found the fat Calories for 1 tablespoon (half a serving). One serving is 2 tablespoons with 16 g of fat: 16 × 9 = 144.

items.explain: Total fat in one serving = 16 g. Calories from fat = 16 × 9 = 144 Calories. That is 144 of the 200 Calories, or 72%, which is why peanut butter is called a high-fat food. Using 4 Calories per gram gives 64, the most common error.

items.prompt: A person eats 4 tablespoons of the peanut butter. Which statement about the saturated fat the person consumes is correct?
options: It is 30% of the Daily Value, so it is high in saturated fat.
It is 15% of the Daily Value, so it is moderate in saturated fat.
It is 60% of the Daily Value, so it is high in saturated fat.
It is 30% of the Daily Value, so it is low because it is under 50%.
why: 15% is for one serving, which is 2 tablespoons. Four tablespoons is 2 servings: 2 × 15% = 30%.
You treated each tablespoon as a serving (4 × 15%). One serving is 2 tablespoons, so 4 tablespoons is only 2 servings.
The 30% is right, but %DV is not judged against 50%. Any value of 20% or more is high.
items.explain: Servings eaten: 4 tablespoons ÷ 2 tablespoons per serving = 2 servings. Saturated fat: 2 × 15% = 30% DV, which is high because it is 20% or more. Multiplying by 4 instead of 2 (60%) is a common error when the serving size is more than one unit.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe how vaccines protect people? Select two answers.
options: A vaccine exposes the immune system to a harmless form or piece of a pathogen.
A vaccine leads the body to make memory cells, so a later infection is fought off faster.
A vaccine is a kind of antibiotic that kills the bacteria already living in the body.
A vaccine works by giving the person a full case of the disease ahead of time.
A vaccine protects only the vaccinated person and has no effect on anyone else nearby.
why: Vaccines are not antibiotics. They train the immune system ahead of time; many vaccines target viruses, which antibiotics cannot affect.
The point of a vaccine is to build immunity without having the disease. It uses a harmless form or piece of the pathogen.
When most people are vaccinated, a contagious pathogen has trouble spreading, which also protects people who are not immune. That is community immunity.
items.explain: A vaccine exposes the immune system to a harmless form or piece of a pathogen, and the body responds by making antibodies and memory cells. If the real pathogen arrives later, the memory cells start a fast, strong response. Vaccines are not antibiotics, they do not cause a full case of the disease, and they help protect the community as well as the individual.

items.prompt: What percent of the workers who were not vaccinated had lab-confirmed flu? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 54 is the number of unvaccinated workers who had flu, not the percent. Divide by the size of that group: 54 ÷ 600 = 0.09 = 9%.
You divided by 400, the number of vaccinated workers. The question asks about the 600 workers who were not vaccinated.
You divided by all 1,000 workers. The percent should be out of the 600 unvaccinated workers only.

items.explain:
Unvaccinated workers: 600. Unvaccinated workers with flu: 54.

54 ÷ 600 = 0.09 = 9%.

For comparison, vaccinated workers: 12 ÷ 400 = 0.03 = 3%.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: The flu rate among vaccinated workers was one-third of the rate among unvaccinated workers.
Unvaccinated workers were 4.5 times as likely to get flu, because 54 is 4.5 times 12.
The vaccine prevented every case of flu among the workers at the company who received it.
The data prove that the vaccine caused the flu in the 12 vaccinated workers who got sick.
why: This compares raw counts from groups of different sizes (400 and 600). Compare rates instead: 3% versus 9%, which is 3 times as likely.
Twelve vaccinated workers still had lab-confirmed flu, so the vaccine did not prevent every case.

The data show only who got sick, not what caused each case. No vaccine protects every person, and flu was spreading during the season, so a few vaccinated workers getting flu does not show the vaccine caused it.
items.explain: Rates: vaccinated 12 ÷ 400 = 3%; not vaccinated 54 ÷ 600 = 9%. 3% is one-third of 9%, so the statement that the vaccinated rate was one-third of the unvaccinated rate is supported. Comparing the counts 54 and 12 ignores that the groups had different sizes. Because workers chose whether to be vaccinated, other differences between the groups could also play a part, which is another reason the data cannot prove cause.

vocab.def: A group of organs that work together to do one major job in the body.
vocab.example: The heart, blood vessels, and blood make up the circulatory system.

vocab.def: Keeping the body's internal conditions stable even when outside conditions change.
vocab.example: Body temperature stays near 37 °C on both hot and cold days.

vocab.def: A cycle in which the body detects a change and responds to it: stimulus, receptor, control center, effector, response.
vocab.example: Skin senses heat, the brain signals sweat glands, sweat cools the body.

vocab.def: A response that reverses a change and brings conditions back toward normal.
vocab.example: Insulin lowers blood sugar after it rises following a meal.

vocab.def: A response that makes a change grow stronger until an event ends it.
vocab.example: Contractions during childbirth get stronger until the baby is born.

vocab.def: The part of the body, often a muscle or gland, that carries out the response in a feedback loop.
vocab.example: Sweat glands are effectors when the body is too hot.

vocab.def: A chemical messenger made by a gland and carried in the blood to other parts of the body.
vocab.example: Insulin is a hormone made by the pancreas.

vocab.def: A unit of energy in food (a food Calorie equals one kilocalorie).
vocab.example: One gram of fat supplies 9 Calories.

vocab.def: A nutrient the body needs in large amounts that supplies energy: carbohydrate, protein, or fat.
vocab.example: Bread is mostly carbohydrate; chicken is mostly protein.

vocab.def: A germ that causes disease, such as a bacterium, virus, fungus, or parasite.
vocab.example: The flu virus is a pathogen.

vocab.def: A tiny pathogen that is not a cell and can reproduce only inside a host's cells; antibiotics do not kill it.
vocab.example: The common cold is caused by viruses.

vocab.def: A medicine that kills bacteria or stops them from growing; it does not work on viruses.
vocab.example: A doctor may prescribe an antibiotic for strep throat, a bacterial infection.

vocab.def: A protein made by white blood cells that attaches to a specific pathogen and helps destroy it.
vocab.example: After a measles infection, the body makes antibodies against the measles virus.

vocab.def: A preparation that trains the immune system to recognize a pathogen without causing the disease.
vocab.example: A flu vaccine helps the body build memory cells against flu viruses.

vocab.def: An animal, such as a mosquito or tick, that carries a pathogen from one host to another.

Body Systems

EndocrineHormones (insulin, glucagon)

Feedback Loop

Stimulus → Receptor → Control center → Effector → Response

Negative ("No, go back"): reverses change. Sweating, shivering, insulin lowers high blood sugar, glucagon raises low blood sugar, kidneys save water.
Positive ("More, more"): increases change until an event ends it. Childbirth, blood clotting.

Nutrition Math

4-4-9: carbohydrate 4, protein 4, fat 9 Calories per gram.

Calories eaten = Calories per serving × servings eaten.

% of Calories from fat = (fat g × 9) ÷ total Calories × 100.

%DV: 5% or less = low; 20% or more = high (2,000-Calorie basis).

Pathogens

Bacteria: living cells; antibiotics work.
Viruses: not cells; need host cells; antibiotics do NOT work.
Fungi, parasites: other medicines.
Spread: air droplets, touch, food/water, vectors (mosquitoes, ticks).

Immunity

1. Barriers (skin, mucus, acid) → 2. General (fever, inflammation, white blood cells) → 3. Targeted (antibodies, memory cells).
Vaccine = memory cells without the disease. Community immunity protects those who are not immune.

Rates: rate per 100,000 = cases ÷ population × 100,000; cases = rate × population ÷ 100,000. Compare rates, not raw counts, when groups differ in size.

Data checklist: title → units → correct row/column → calculate → choose what the data actually show (pattern ≠ proof of cause). Mean: add values, divide by how many. Percent change: (new − old) ÷ old × 100.
